articles.title: Calls for judge to be stood down after teen avoids jail for rape
articles.author: Lily Nothling and Jade Toomey

paras.en: A teenager was last week given an 18-month suspended sentence after pleading guilty to rape.
ACT Supreme Court Justice Andrew Muller said the teenager's lack of sexual experience and "limited insight" into Australia's societal norms were factors in his sentencing decision.
The ACT Director of Public Prosecutions will consider appealing against the sentence.
The ACT Director of Public Prosecutions will consider appealing against a controversial sentence handed to a teenage boy who pinned down and raped a young woman he met at a Canberra house party.
Warning: This story contains descriptions of sexual assault.
The teenager, who was 16 at the time of the rape, pleaded guilty in the ACT Children's Court to sexual intercourse without consent.
The now-18-year-old avoided jail time and instead received an 18-month suspended sentence upon entering a good behaviour order.

In sentencing last week, ACT Supreme Court Justice Andrew Muller accepted the teenager's "prior lack of sexual experience and inevitably limited insight into societal norms in Australia … are factors mitigating his moral culpability".
The teenager had moved to Canberra from Bhutan in February 2025, six months before the assault occurred.
He cannot be named because be he was a minor at the time of the offence.
He has spent one night in custody since the offending in August 2025.
The sentence has sparked fierce public backlash from parts of the Canberra community.
A petition calling for the removal of Justice Muller had on Wednesday received 4,000 signatures.
Petition organiser Joanne Matthews said she wanted the justice system to reconsider the sentence.
"They are supposed to reflect what society wants, and this is not what society wants,"
Ms Matthews, a Canberra resident, said she was disappointed the court considered the teen's short time in Australia to be a mitigating factor.
"Does this give permission for anyone coming in to say, 'well, I'm ignorant of the law, I can commit these horrendous crimes and that's okay'?" she said.
A separate petition sponsored by Canberra Liberals MLA Peter Cain launched on Tuesday calling for a public inquiry into the ACT's sentencing framework for sexual violence.

"The community needs assurance that sentencing outcomes are justified, assessments of reoffending risk are rigorous, and mitigating factors do not diminish victims' entitlement to justice or community safety," the petition, which has received 170 signatures, said.
The office of ACT Attorney-General Tara Cheyne declined to comment on the case, saying any decision about an appeal was a matter for the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP).
An ACT government spokesperson said the territory's legislative framework was designed to safeguard the independence of the DPP.

"Under the Director of Public Prosecutions Act 1990, the attorney-general may issue directions or guidelines to the director only on matters of a general nature and cannot direct how the DPP should act in a specific case,"
'Unclear' what offender is sorry for: judge
During sentencing, the court heard the teen and his 18-year-old victim had met at a party in Holt where they kissed before he asked her to go for a walk a few houses away.
He then pinned her down, ripped her clothes, and repeatedly sexually assaulted her.
The victim, who also cannot be named, said she "just froze" and told the offender, "please stop, I don't want this".
She estimated the offending lasted for 20 minutes.
The victim told the court she wanted to run away but was scared the offender would hurt her.
Justice Muller said he acknowledged "troubling concerns" about the teen's insights.
"I have no doubt he feels sorry," he said.

"But whether he feels sorry because of the impact these charges have had in his own life, or whether he feels sorry because he realises what he did was wrong and recognises the abhorrence with which the community regards his wrongful behaviour is a little unclear,"

The offender, who is currently completing Year 12, had previously been issued a restraining order for punching another student at school and had admitted to photographing another student using the toilet.
Speaking broadly about sentencing in sexual assault cases, ACT Victims of Crime Commissioner Juliette Ford said the lifelong impact a crime had on victims was not always understood.
The commissioner said victims generally "have faith in the criminal justice process [and] they don't want what happened to them to happen to someone else."
"It is very important then that the outcomes do properly reflect the impact of the harm caused to them," he said.

articles.title: Rex grounds two routes 10 months after $60m rescue package
articles.author: Marina Trajkovich and Xanthe Gregory

paras.en: Rex Airlines will suspend its Orange and Port Macquarie services from October 25.
The decision comes less than a year after the carrier was sold in a deal that featured a $60 million rescue package and a further $108 million to restructure Commonwealth debt.
The airline says it will monitor fuel costs and reinstate the routes it becomes commercially viable.
Less than a year after it was sold with the aid of a federal government rescue package, embattled airline Regional Express (Rex) has grounded flights to two NSW destinations.
The carrier announced that flights to and from Sydney and Port Macquarie on the Mid North Coast and Orange in the Central West will be indefinitely halted from October 25.
Independent MP Andrew Gee, whose federal electorate takes in Orange, described the decision as a "real shock".
"It feels like a slap in the face or a kick in the guts for the whole region after everyone called for so much support and so much pressure was put on the government to deliver it," he said.
A Commonwealth bailout allowed the airline to keep flying its regional routes and, in late 2025, it was bought by US-based air services company Air T.
The sale was endorsed by the federal government, which backed the bid with a $60 million support package and an additional $108 million to help restructure existing Commonwealth debt.

In exchange for that support Air T made commitments to increase the number of aircraft in service, maintain an ongoing level of service to regional Australia, and increase frequencies of profitable flights across its network.
The ABC has contacted Air T for comment.
A spokesperson for Federal Transport Minister Catherine King issued a statement acknowledging the Rex decision would be "be disappointing for many".
"In return for support from the Australian Government, Air T agreed to a set of regional commitments aimed at maintaining Rex's services to regional Australia," the spokesperson said.
"Notwithstanding these changes, Rex continues to operate one of Australia's largest regional air networks.
"The Government continues to work closely with Rex to understand market challenges and to monitor Rex's compliance with regional commitments."
The statement noted that customers in both regional destinations would still be able to fly to and from Sydney on different carriers.
A statement issued by Rex said the suspensions were indefinite, and affected customers would be offered "refunds or re-bookings".

"The environment of entrenched high fuel prices driven by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, together with lack of demand, do not make these routes commercially viable at this time," the statement said.
REX said it would monitor the situation and consider reinstating the routes "once fuel prices decrease to a level that makes it commercially viable for flights to resume".
The carrier said it remained "committed to serving regional and remote Australia".
In May, the airline cut two services in Tasmania and scaled back a service to Mildura in Victoria's north-west.
Port Macquarie Mayor Adam Roberts said the area's $700 million annual visitor economy would be hit by the Rex decision.
"The reality is that it has a significant flow-on effect to our community," he said.
"Living in a regional area, we absolutely need these vital services."
Cr Adams said whether airport staff would lose jobs remained unclear, but discussions were underway to mitigate impacts.
"The state and federal governments need to look at what's happening here and ask the question [whether] they could potentially help us stabilise our potential for travel," he said.
"If it's a grant fund or if it's a carrot to entice more airlines to use this airport, we're already having some peripheral conversations."
Orange Mayor Tony Mileto is pessimistic about the prospect of the service ever being reinstated.
"I don't think they'll be backflipping on the decision," he said.
Cr Mileto said there was clearly demand among the other airlines that serviced the airport, including Qantas and Link Airways.
"I think it's for Rex to answer as to why more people weren't taking up their flights," he said.
Cr Mileto said the council would request a meeting with those competitors to ensure their services were at least maintained.
"Air travel is vitally important to Orange and we want to ensure that people feel confident there will be flights available should they require them," he said.
Earlier this year, the Orange City Council received a slice of $4.8 million from the Commonwealth to cover Rex's unpaid debts to regional councils.

articles.title: Trump's new press secretary faces questions about her legal credentials
articles.author: Hanan Dervisevic

paras.en: An inaugural, albeit short, White House press briefing offered a glimpse into how Trump's latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will approach the notoriously difficult role.
The 41-year-old spent much of the 14-minute appearance reading from prepared remarks before taking just three questions, all from conservative-leaning outlets.
Zacharia's debut comes after the departure of Karoline Leavitt, who became known for her combative and high-profile briefing style.

Zacharia, a conservative commentator named to the role on Friday, opened her first session by reading, at a notably slow pace, a lengthy list of what she described as achievements made by the "energetic" US President Donald Trump.
She highlighted Trump's recent campaign rallies and his policies on energy, tariffs, immigration and more since he returned to office.
"Everyday Americans are showing up in droves to attend rallies because of President Trump's America-first agenda of lower taxes, higher wages and one of my favourites, secure borders," Zacharia said.
"Attendance is at record highs as enthusiastic and hardworking Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans.
"It's not hard to see why. President Trump is fighting and delivering for American workers every minute of every day."
Typically, a lengthy question-and-answer session follows a press secretary's opening remarks, often spanning dozens of questions from reporters.
But Zacharia took questions from just three reporters, starting with right-wing website Breitbart, an outlet frequently accused of misinformation.
The next questions went to Fox News and the Daily Mail.
When asked by Fox whether the administration had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Zacharia was unable to provide an answer.
"I'll have to get back to you on that," she said.
Zacharia raised eyebrows when she was asked about her legal qualifications on the White House South Lawn alongside Trump after the briefing.
"What state did she pass the bar exam in? You said she is an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" the reporter asked.
Trump turned to Zacharia and repeated the question.
A White House official later did not directly answer questions about whether Zacharia had passed a US bar exam, which is required in the US to practice law.

Her LinkedIn profile said she worked as an associate in the International Practice Team at Zhong Lun law firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013, however non-citizens can not sit China's national bar exam and cannot engage in legal practice involving Chinese law.
Pepperdine University confirmed Zacharia graduated from its law school in 2011, but there has been no confirmation so far she passed the California bar exam.
The briefing drew criticism from several former White House officials, who questioned both its length and Zacharia's performance.
Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci joked on X: "The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci."
Scaramucci famously lasted 11 days in the role during Trump's first administration.
Sarah Matthews, who served as deputy White House press secretary during Trump's first term, described the debut as "rather underwhelming".
"Three questions, including one from the new media seat, and a heavy reliance on her notes. Not exactly in command of the briefing room," Matthews wrote on X.
Former Clinton administration press secretary Joe Lockhart told CNN it was "a little bizarre" to usher Zacharia into the briefing room for such a short appearance.
"I'm not sure what they were hoping to accomplish, but I don't think they built any confidence in her ability to go forward," he said.
Meanwhile, former Biden press secretary Jen Psaki described the briefing on X as "basically an SNL skit … except it wasn't".
Mistakenly calls her husband 'my president'
One of the lighter moments came when Zacharia accidentally referred to her husband as "my president" while discussing her family.
"The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable. So my president, excuse me, my husband ‒ that's a good one," she said.
Speaking to reporters before his trip to Alaska, Trump praised his new press secretary's performance.
"I thought she did excellent. She did very good," he said.
The White House also issued a statement.
"Today, Katie Zacharia delivered a commanding inaugural press briefing as the 37th White House Press Secretary," the White House statement read.

"The briefing, which generated wall-to-wall coverage, served as a strong introduction to her tenure and highlighted the Trump Administration's record of delivering historic successes for the American people."

articles.title: IN PHOTOS | France student protests spread across Europe

paras.en: IN PHOTOS | France student protests spread across Europe
Weeks of protest over school conditions, education costs spread to Albania, Greece
Nationwide protests by high school students over education in France have spread to other parts of Europe in recent weeks.
Student organizers in Albania said Tuesday's nationwide protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
The protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at Albania's Education Ministry in Tirana, and police fired tear gas and water cannons in response as the demonstration turned violent.
Police officers detained several protesters.

High school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades in France, demanding more teachers and better facilities. Below, they, along with teachers and parents, block a street near the Lycée Hélène Boucher high school in Paris on Tuesday.
More than 161,000 people took to the streets of major French cities, according to Interior Ministry figures. That was down from 266,000 on a similar day of action a week ago.

While most demonstrators marched peacefully, riot police charged protesters and fired tear gas in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Nantes, while a fringe of protesters lit fires, vandalized property and hurled objects at police.
Below, French CRS riot police push barriers to apprehend a protester amid clashes during a demonstration in Paris.
A masked protester attempts to kick a tear gas canister amid clashes during the demonstration.
University students gather outside the Finance Ministry in Athens on Tuesday to protest rising rents and the lack of affordable student housing.
(Thanassis Stavrakis/The Associated Press)
Tents staged at Syntagma Square near parliament during a protest in Athens.

articles.title: OpenAI engineer arrested, accused of planting listening device inside company's office

paras.en: OpenAI engineer arrested, accused of planting listening device inside company's office
OpenAI says it used AI to identify suspect

U.S. federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the U.S. Justice Department said on Tuesday.

The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name did not elicit a response, and it was not immediately clear who his lawyer was.

OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on Sept. 30, according to the department.

The thumb-sized device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about Sept. 28, but its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan's personal bag.
OpenAI said in an X post that it had used its internal AI models to identify the individual responsible for planting the device and trace its origins.
The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the company said.
OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi embassy in the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

"Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology," FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through Sept. 16, according to the FBI complaint. He has been a legal permanent resident of the U.S. since September 2020.
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 US fine and three years of supervised release.
- OpenAI scraps release of new AI model over safety concerns
- OpenAI flags 6 new examples of 'concerning' AI behaviour
Alfozan studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley, according to his LinkedIn profile. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft.
Reuters could not independently verify the details mentioned in his LinkedIn profile.

Separately, the tech industry outlet the Information reported that OpenAI was in early talks to acquire Trail of Bits, a startup that identifies and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software. The talks were ongoing and could fall apart, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.
OpenAI and Trail of Bits did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers after an investigation found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information.

The statement came after the researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture that had allowed researchers to raise safety concerns.

articles.title: Grad student accused of trying to flee U.S. after police questioned her about alleged poisoning

paras.en: Grad student accused of trying to flee U.S. after police questioned her about alleged poisoning
Microbiology grad student alleged to have poisoned tea of University of Wyoming colleague

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents, then tried to flee the U.S. after police questioned her.

Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were "multiple" laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police.

Investigators say Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the alleged victim, who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work Wang had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles.
It's claimed the poison was first detected when the wife of the alleged victim and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations have left him reeling. He said he was uncertain if the alleged victim will fully recover.

"It's been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student's life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that," Gomelsky told The Associated Press. "That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career."
Wang has no attorney listed in court documents. The Associated Press tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.

The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as K.T., began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical acrylamide in the coffee maker's water.
K.T. and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie, Wyo.

Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through K.T.'s desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded "taking photos and manipulating notebooks" on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer's affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
Police said Wang had asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer.
A carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide, which can be acutely toxic in high doses, is also used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she "had not used acrylamide in years."

A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of "multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials," according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to "significantly increase" her $200,000 US bond upon extradition.

Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved "new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment," according to the affidavit.
Wang "was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.," the affidavit alleges.
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.

Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague's success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a conference in August, Gomelsky said.
Later that month he went to the campus health clinic with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness.
The student also said he had noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said, and that when he washed the coffee maker the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.

The water from the coffee maker was boiled down to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit. The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.

Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is "not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere," Sumaya said.
The alleged victim was working on "a pretty promising cancer therapy method," Sumaya added.
The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.
"Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it's unclear if he'll fully recover or not," the professor said.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 US fine.
It's not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors' request and raised bond to $1.5 million US, cash only.

articles.title: India: Can 'cockroaches' threaten Modi's political grip?

paras.en: India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) may have anticipated pushback from the government after its first round of protests in July, but the scale of barricading and detentions that greeted its leaders in a fortress-like New Delhi on October 10 was unlike anything they had anticipated.

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In its latest round of agitation, they are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were reportedly removed from electoral rolls nationwide.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, accompanied by co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, was detained from the plane in which he landed in the national capital on Saturday.

Meanwhile, police were stationed outside the homes of several other faces associated with the movement, including social media personality Dhruv Rathee, who has nearly 20 million followers on Instagram.

In central Delhi, buses were loaded with protesters, many of whom were taken to far-flung centers, where they were kept for hours. According to local media, at least 3,000 people were detained across the city.
How the government is handling the protests
The protests come as Modi marks 25 uninterrupted years leading elected governments, first in Gujarat state as chief minister and then as prime minister of India.

Ironically, "this celebration has happened at the time when he's politically at his weakest," Delhi-based writer Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told DW. Mukhopadhyay is the author of Modi's 2013 biography "Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times."

He contrasted the government's current response with its approach in July, when thousands of young protesters took to the streets to demand the resignation of Modi's education minister over repeated exam paper leaks.
At the time, authorities had used batons, detentions and pellets to disperse the crowds gathered in central Delhi, which had been on the streets for days.

This time, authorities shifted to mass security deployments and preemptive action on a large scale. This included notices to those associated with earlier protests, transport cuts, the internet cutoff and airport arrests.

"The government has learned from its previous experience. They didn't allow people to sit at Jantar Mantar for any length of time, so it couldn't balloon," Pearl Pandya, senior analyst for Asia at global monitor ACLED, told DW.

"What's worrying is whether this becomes a playbook for the future — that you are not allowed to protest in the first place," she added, referring to the government's decision to remove the 18th-century observatory Jantar Mantar in central Delhi from the list of designated protest sites.
Authorities, however, have announced three new designated protest sites in the national capital.
Mukhopadhyay had a different reading of the situation. "The scale of this deployment is actually a defeat for Mr. Modi," he said.
Mukhopadhyay argued that it was already a setback for the government if it was forced to deploy security forces on such a scale in response to protests from a completely new socio-political movement.
Despite the momentum, the CJP has not been able to replicate its success from July, with the protests against Kumar being led primarily by opposition leaders and student organizations.
"Education was far more of a cross-cutting issue... the right to vote is still seen as an intrinsically political one, where it's the opposition versus the BJP," Pandya said.
The CJP, however, has long maintained that it is non-political. This is often cited as the reason for them amassing such a large following of young followers.
Mukhopadhyay criticized that stance, saying: "You cannot raise issues about electoral neutrality... without saying that these are political issues."
Despite the differences between the previous round of CJP protests in July and the current wave of demonstrations, sociologist Surinder Singh Jodhka emphasized continuity.

"I don't think they're qualitatively different. Once again, young people are the ones who are mobilized, and they are much more encouraged because the earlier round of protests was successful," he told DW. "And it's also asking similar questions about institutions, about democracy, about transparency and accountability."
"There is a new hope for those who had earlier given up on India, and felt like the right wing was in complete control," Jodhka added.

Dismissing comparisons with volatile protests in neighboring Nepal and Bangladesh, which brought down their governments, the analysts pointed to India's strong institutions as a safeguard against a dramatic change of government.

"India has had a very strong state system and state institutions," Jodhka explained, highlighting that even the opposition parties were asking for "the revival of institutions, rather than an overthrow of the state."
Pandya also stated that faith in the judiciary "would prevent these protests from tipping over into a popular revolution which unseats the government."
Nevertheless, she said, sustained discontent "might come to bite the government in 2029... or before that in the state elections."
It could also erode Modi's popularity, which has been a defining feature of Indian politics over the past decade, the expert indicated.
For Mukhopadhyay, the most troubling aspect of the current protests is the erosion of the electoral body's credibility.
Recalling the pride he felt when he registered to vote at 21, he drew comparisons with young Indian voters today. "The youngsters are now fighting for their vote."

articles.title: Ukraine and the US: What's next after Trump's diesel deal with Russia?

paras.en: The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president."
The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami.

"I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners."
This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards."

The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports.

The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic.

"Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything."

All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election.
Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices.

"Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said.
Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine."

Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump.
Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action.

"Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said.

At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this.
Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric.
"You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington.

Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran.

Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products.
Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections.
"The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said.

The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China.

Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil.

"Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said.
He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal

paras.en: The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.

This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap.
What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine?

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections.
"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday.
"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.
"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.

Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, meanwhile, said he was counting on "our MAGA president" — a reference to Andrzej Duda of the rival PiS party whom Trump has often praised — to use his "friendship" with Trump to do two things.

"Number one: to secure a permanent US base in Poland. And, number two: to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor, and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression, and you end the war by convincing the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," Sikorski said.
Norway's Espen Barth Eide said it was important to focus on the actions of the last four years, also welcoming Monday's latest round of Russian sanctions.

"I feel that what we've done over the last years ... all of this is a very strong signal that Europe, together with Canada and — on most good days — also with the US, we are sending a very clear message to Putin," Eide said.

Facing criticism at home as well, Trump on Tuesday said that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. He also said that other countries would be buying Russian diesel as part of the deal he announced, without being deemed to breach US sanctions, rather than the US buying it itself. This contradicted or possibly corrected his earlier statements.
Wadephul: Starlink sabotage shows Europe 'in the crosshairs' of Russia
Wadephul also told reporters during his visit that he had spoken with his opposite number Sikorski about the investigations into a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month.

Two people with Turkish citizenship were arrested in Germany in the southwestern town of Nürtingen, not far from Stuttgart, on Monday. Based on comments from Polish officials, they are suspected of connections with organized criminality but are thought to have been working on behalf of Russia.
Wadephul said that this and other hybrid incidents across the continent showed that "we are in Russia's crosshairs."
The satellite-based Starlink internet service is used extensively by Ukraine's military and so the fire was thought to be targeting accessibility across the border in the warzone.
"We're being attacked and it's not just happening in Ukraine but all across Europe," Wadephul said. "That means we must strengthen our cooperation."
But he also said that the arrests in Germany, which will likely lead to an exatradition process, showed how the security systems were working — both at the policing and intelligence-gathering levels.
He said he did not believe Russia would succeed in "dividing us" with such campaigns, saying that instead he expected they would galvanize European allies.
A private Polish broadcaster meanwhile reported two further arrests in Germany on Tuesday, although German authorities did not immediately comment on them.
Miliband praises Zelenskyy, but says 'let us take seriously' energy ceasefire idea

UK Foreign Secretary Miliband praised Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine.

However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.
"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need," Miliband said.
Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.
Wadephul added that, if possible, any such efforts to broker a partial ceasefire should also seek to incoporate grain exports and shipments in the Black Sea, particuarly to North Africa.

"This is still necessary. And let us please not forget this and urge Russia also to be ready to enlarge the ceasefire, not only for the energy sector but also for the Black Sea. Because this is needed to stop a lot of people in North Africa from falling into hunger," he said.
If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

articles.title: UN official says ‘window of opportunity’ for peace in DR Congo

paras.en: A senior United Nations official has told the Security Council there is a “window of opportunity” for peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, a mineral-rich region plagued by decades of conflict.
Huang Xia, the UN special envoy for the impacted Great Lakes Region, on Tuesday said that both US- and Qatar-led peace processes have achieved “notable progress”.
However, “despite this sustained diplomatic effort, the security and humanitarian situation in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has continued to worsen”, he added.
Several parties, including the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group and the Congolese army, have clashed in the territory, prompting a series of international diplomatic efforts.
Huang stressed the “urgency of seizing the window of opportunity, which is currently offered by the increased alignment of peace efforts”.
“Such a window does not remain open indefinitely,” he said.
“I therefore urge all parties to translate commitments into verifiable actions, and to place their trust in confidence built through deeds rather than through declarations.”
The Congolese government and the M23 signed a commitment towards a ceasefire in Doha in July 2025. The DRC and Rwanda also formalised a US-brokered peace deal in December in Washington, DC.
However, fighting has continued on the ground.
New talks were held in August in Switzerland, involving representatives from the United States, Qatar and the African Union.
Huang said the UN would facilitate a meeting on October 18 in Zambia’s capital, Lusaka, between the defence ministers of Burundi, the DRC, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania.

articles.title: Singapore’s economy grows more than 5 percent amid AI boom

paras.en: Singapore’s economy grew more than 5 percent in the most recent quarter, continuing an AI-fuelled boom that has made the city-state one of the fastest-growing advanced economies.

Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 5.4 percent year-on-year between July and September, down from a 6.2 percent expansion in the second quarter, according to advance government estimates released on Wednesday.
Manufacturing, which is dominated by the city-state’s semiconductor industry, grew 7.5 percent, according to the estimates from the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

Increased output in “electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters” drove growth, the ministry said, offsetting declines in the chemicals and biomedical sectors.
Construction, including AI-related investments such as data centres, expanded 8.8 per cent, according to the figures.
Despite the heady expansion, Singapore’s central bank left its monetary policy settings untouched in its latest announcement on Wednesday, citing expectations that AI demand will cool in 2027.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore, which manages monetary policy through currency exchange rates rather than interest rates, said it expected core inflation to average 1.5–2.0 percent in 2026.

“Global AI-driven growth is expected to ease in the latter half of next year from its current exceptional pace, while higher interest rates, amid elevated inflation in the advanced economies, would weigh on final demand growth,” the central bank said in a statement.
Singapore is a major global player in the booming chip sector, a position that has helped it weather choppy economic conditions, including the energy shock prompted by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The Southeast Asian city-state accounts for roughly 10 percent of global semiconductor output and 20 percent of semiconductor equipment production, according to government figures.

Yeow Hwee Chua, an assistant professor of economics at Nanyang Technological University, described Singapore’s economic performance as “impressive for a high-income economy, especially given the uncertain global environment”.
“The global technology investment boom has been an important driver,” Chua told Al Jazeera.
“Strong demand for electronics has supported manufacturing and related wholesale trade, illustrating how Singapore benefits from its position in global supply chains,” he said.
Singapore’s economy is expected to grow 5 percent in 2026, according to the IMF’s latest economic forecast, faster than any other advanced economy except Taiwan.
The city-state’s GDP grew 5 percent in 2025, its second straight year of growth above 5 percent – the first such streak since 2010 and 2011.

articles.title: China and North Korea to open New Yalu River Bridge, state media reports

paras.en: China and North Korea will officially open the New Yalu River Bridge to traffic on Thursday, China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reports.

China completed its side of the bridge in 2014, hoping to boost trade ties. However, North Korea left its side unfinished for years as relations soured after Beijing supported United Nations sanctions over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests.
The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea also opened earlier this month.

China’s exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3bn last year, a 25 percent increase from the previous year. Chinese President Xi Jinping was welcomed in Pyongyang in June for the first time since 2019.
Since 2018, Beijing has tried to repair ties with Pyongyang, which also briefly began improving relations with Washington around the same time.

The China-North Korea relationship was forged during the Korean War. In 1961, the two countries signed the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which remains China’s only formal military alliance.
The treaty contains a mutual defence clause committing either side to assist the other if one comes under armed attack.

Although China was North Korea’s main diplomatic partner and protector for decades, relations strained after Beijing in 2017 supported tightening sanctions on Pyongyang for its nuclear weapons programme.
Analysts say North Korea’s recent growing relationship with Russia may have changed the balance of Pyongyang’s diplomatic dependence, reducing its reliance on Beijing.

North Korea and Russia signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in 2024, including a mutual defence provision. Military and political ties between the two countries have grown considerably stronger, with North Korea deploying thousands of troops to fight in Russia’s war on Ukraine.

United States President Donald Trump also signalled an interest in repairing relations with Pyongyang last month, after his talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un abruptly ended in 2019. In his second term, Trump has floated meeting Kim again, though no official meeting has been set.
North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, exchanges with China could arguably involve goods North Korea needs to develop its civilian economy, analysts have said.

articles.title: How NATO plans to combat potential attacks on the alliance from Russia
articles.author: Steve Inskeep

paras.en: How NATO plans to combat potential attacks on the alliance from Russia
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with former U.S. Assistant Secretary for European Affairs Dan Hamilton about NATO's detailed plans to counter any possible Russian attack on the alliance.

Dan Hamilton has been listening with us. He served as deputy assistant secretary for European affairs at the State Department in the 1990s. He was responsible for NATO security issues. Welcome to the program.
INSKEEP: Why is NATO needing to talk about its defense strategy against a Russian attack now?

HAMILTON: I think that the - as Teri just said, you know, the allies in Europe are uneasy. They're uneasy about the continued U.S. commitment to the alliance. They're nervous about Russia's not only conventional war against Ukraine, but the uptick in these unconventional assaults all across the rest of Europe. You know, the U.S. B-1 bombers had to relocate back to the U.S. from the U.K. because of a suspected assault on a U.K. base. There is sabotage at Leipzig Airport in Germany. There's been arson attacks, cyberattacks. So they wanted to hear directly that NATO has a strategy and that NATO, you know, has got it, as General Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Forum.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: INSKEEP: Would you talk me through that threat? I mean, when you mentioned the British airbase, of course, that's something that British authorities blame on Iran, not Russia, but some of the others could be traced to Russia. Is there a way for Russia to seriously attack and gain ground in Europe without the full-scale ground offensive that didn't work very well for them in Ukraine?

HAMILTON: Well, the - it's hard to see Russia launching some full-scale attack, especially if it's bogged down right now in Ukraine and any mass movement of forces, of course, would be detected early by NATO. But, you know, think about what Russia's goals might be, is to demoralize European governments, distract them from attention to Ukraine or that they question their own policies to supply Ukraine with armaments that they might then need and get European publics to question their own government support for Ukraine. You know, the Leipzig attack in Germany is - was in a German state right next to crucial state elections in East Germany, where the far right gained significantly, just a couple of weeks ago, and they all have a pro-Russian attitude there.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So instead of thinking of assault, think of a small scenario. You know, you could have armed individuals without insignia just crossing a river in a Baltic state like Narva, Estonia, which is right on the Russian border. Would NATO go to war because of something like that? Is there a consensus among allies on how you respond? These kinds of scenarios are what keep NATO officials up at night because it might be a political move by Putin sometimes to split the alliance rather than...
INSKEEP: When you talked about armed men without - armed troops without insignia crossing a border, of course, that's the way Russia seized Crimea once upon a time.
INSKEEP: Does the United States in some way undermine the alliance by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, something that clearly dismays Europeans?

HAMILTON: Well, they're just at cross-purposes, you know, for the president to announce this, even though there is a U.S. law, as a bipartisan group of U.S. senators said, to stop - that prevents U.S. dollars from financing Putin's war. He went ahead with that announcement anyway. At the same time, as Teri mentioned, the EU yesterday launched the biggest batch of sanctions against Russia that it has since the 2022 invasion. So we are definitely working at cross-purposes here.
INSKEEP: Does it surprise you that the sanctions have not ultimately brought Russia down? Their economy was hurt for a while but seems to have gradually recovered.

HAMILTON: It's a wartime economy. It's being propped up by Chinese support, and I don't think it can sustain itself if it keeps going like this. So the sanctions do hurt, and they force Putin to make tough choices.
INSKEEP: Dan Hamilton is a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Institute of Johns Hopkins University. Thanks very much for your time.
(SOUNDBITE OF EL TEN ELEVEN'S "THINKING LOUDLY")

articles.title: Trump's diesel deal with Putin angers Europe
articles.author: Teri Schultz

paras.en: Trump's diesel deal with Putin angers Europe
President Trump's diesel deal with Russia sparks European fury, as Ukraine's President Zelenskyy questions Washington's motives and allies vow to keep pressure on Moscow.
Leaders in Europe do not like President Trump's latest moves in the war in Ukraine.

Yeah. Trump demanded that Ukraine stop its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump also said that there was a ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure, which neither Ukraine nor Russia seem to know about. The president also lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, even as Europeans impose new sanctions on the Russian military complex.
INSKEEP: Teri Schultz is following all this from a European security conference in Warsaw, Poland. Welcome.
INSKEEP: So what is it about the president's statements that concerns allies of Ukraine?

SCHULTZ: I think there's just really no faith in these moves by the White House, Steve. You know, President Zelenskyy spoke here remotely in Warsaw and said that even as this ceasefire was announced by President Trump, Ukrainian oil refineries were being bombed. So European officials and experts treated this basically as one more attempt by the White House to pressure Ukraine in favor of Russia. Now, one of the strongest reactions came from Trump's former Ukraine envoy, Keith Kellogg, who shared what he would advise Zelenskyy to do in quite colorful language.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: KEITH KELLOGG: I'd burn down every one of the goddamn refineries that Russia has today. Take them all out. And I said (ph), you make them pay the price. You take it home. It's a military target. Take those targets out.
SCHULTZ: Now, Kellogg left his position in January and has been pretty outspoken about his support for Kyiv since.

INSKEEP: OK. So how are Europeans responding to this other development? The United States has very high diesel fuel prices, and the president suddenly announced an agreement of some sort for the U.S. to buy diesel fuel from Russia.

SCHULTZ: More of the same from the European perspective, but in the meantime, the European Union even intensified its efforts to stem the Kremlin's war effort. Now, it takes a long time to tee up sanctions, so this is not in reaction specifically to these latest U.S. moves, but the EU just imposed its largest-ever package of sanctions against almost 1,600 individuals and companies related to Russia's military industry. And while it appears that no one knew in advance about Trump's diesel deal, analyst Majda Ruge from the European Council on Foreign Relations says it wasn't exactly a surprise.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MAJDA RUGE: Trump's personal desire for economic reset with Russia and announcing business deals has really been the only consistent element of Trump's Russia-Ukraine policies.
INSKEEP: Let me come back to this security conference where you're at. What are NATO officials saying, the North Atlantic alliance?

SCHULTZ: Well, there's a lot of concern in Europe about U.S. plans to withdraw troops and military assets. So U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich - he's NATO's supreme allied commander Europe - used this conference to make sure there's no misunderstanding in Moscow that NATO's resolve is weakening. He unveiled what he called the theory of victory, describing how NATO would use its entire range of capabilities to respond to any attack.

ALEXUS GRYNKEWICH: Our alliance exists to preserve peace, but let there be no doubt, should war come, we will block, blunt any attack. And then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us. We're rehearsed, and we're ready.

SCHULTZ: And Grynkewich's speech comes as Europe is experiencing an increasing number of Russian threats, including sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation. And that's in addition to the concerns about the U.S. commitment. So this speech was definitely meant to reassure allies that NATO's got things covered in all contingencies.
INSKEEP: Teri Schultz is reporting from Warsaw. Thanks so much.

articles.title: How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market?
articles.author: Willa Rubin

paras.en: How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market?
The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the U.S. in September. Can President Trump's deal for Russia to release more diesel onto the market bring the price down?

OK, there are plenty of legal and political questions surrounding President Trump's deal to get Russia to release more oil to the U.S. and global markets. And, of course, a lot of Americans are wondering how that deal could affect the price of diesel. NPR energy reporter Willa Rubin joins us now to talk about all of this. Hi, Willa.
CHANG: Hi. OK, so give us the lay of the land here. What is happening with the price of diesel in the U.S. right now?

RUBIN: Well, it hit an all-time high a few weeks ago, which is important for the U.S. economy. You know, our industrial supply chain relies on diesel, tractors that farmers use, trucks that bring your food from farms eventually to the grocery store. If diesel is expensive, that contributes to the price of everything that you buy. Now, the price of a gallon has come down a little bit since that September high. On average, it's now $6.27, according to AAA, but that is still really high. Diesel is about $2.60 more than this time last year.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: CHANG: OK, and explain this to me. What did President Trump say about how he expects this deal would work exactly?

RUBIN: Yeah, so in a post on Truth Social on Friday, President Trump said that Russia had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and to global markets immediately. But, like, is that a little or a lot in terms of how much the U.S. actually uses?
RUBIN: Yeah. So to put this in context for the rest of October, Will O'Neil is an analyst at S&P Global Energy. He's a follower of all things diesel.
WILL O'NEIL: Because I could even do some quick Excel math. So 300,000 tons over the course of 20 days is...
RUBIN: I love that you broke out an Excel spreadsheet mid conversation (laughter).
O'NEIL: That's what I do. That's my job.

RUBIN: So he figured out that if you convert tons to barrels and the U.S. uses up to 4 million barrels a day, the entire amount expected to be released in October adds up to about half the diesel the U.S. uses in just one day.
RUBIN: Drops in the bucket. And if you do some more math using the entire amount expected to be released over the coming months, O'Neil said it adds up to about nine days' worth.
CHANG: Let me ask you this. Is Russia really in any position to export all of this diesel?
RUBIN: Analysts in the U.S. don't know, but what...
RUBIN: ...They do know is that Russia's refinery capacity has been significantly reduced by Ukraine's strikes. O'Neil says it's probably reduced 40- to 45% of their capacity.
O'NEIL: Ukrainian drone strikes have taken so much of its refining capacity offline that it just simply doesn't have the diesel production to send to global markets.

RUBIN: He says this deal does not change that reality. Russia has had an export ban since July, though they partially lifted it on Saturday. Also worth noting, the U.S. has had wide ranging sanctions on Russian energy since its full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. On Friday, the Treasury Department announced it was temporarily waiving sanctions on diesel for about six months. And this has gotten some pushback from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle. This is a really complicated situation, Ailsa, with a lot of moving parts.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: CHANG: Clearly. OK, if Russia really can bring this diesel to market, could that help lower prices in the U.S., you think, eventually?

RUBIN: Big picture, what drives diesel prices is global demand. And there's a global diesel deficit right now. A good chunk of that is due to the war in Iran. Claudio Galimberti is a partner and chief economist at Rystad Energy. He says the world is missing up to 1.5 million barrels per day that normally come from the Middle East and another million barrels that would come from Russia.
CLAUDIO GALIMBERTI: So it's a huge gap, and this deal only address (ph) a very small portion of that.
CHANG: OK, Willa, I'm no economist, but it sounds like he doesn't think this will really lower prices all that much. Am I getting that right?
RUBIN: Yeah. Analysts told me we will only start to see big meaningful drops in prices by solving these bottlenecks by ending the wars.
CHANG: That is NPR's Willa Rubin. Thank you so much, Willa.
