paras.zh: 当然，OpenAI 结果的新颖性并不意味着它没有受到西班牙项目的影响。事实上，OpenAI 最初使用了较小的代理团队来证明中间结果，一些专家表示，这个更温和的团队确实遵循了该计划。但 10,000 名特工群体显然意识到需要一条不同的路径来完成这项工作。当然，尽管 OpenAI 坚称其模型无法看到 Buckmaster 的特定用户数据，但 LLM 的“黑匣子”性质意味着我们可能永远不会知道群体的确切推理链。

paras.en: “I honestly don’t see a factual resolution of this,” says Camillo De Lellis, a mathematician at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J. “It’s not anymore a matter of clearly verifiable mathematical facts.”
paras.zh: 新泽西州普林斯顿高等研究院的数学家卡米洛·德·莱利斯 (Camillo De Lellis) 表示：“老实说，我看不到这个问题的事实解决方案。这不再是一个可以明确验证的数学事实的问题。”

paras.en: What’s important, and perhaps a harbinger of math’s future, is how long it took experts to realize all this. When OpenAI revealed its landmark achievement on September 8, company officials clearly and repeatedly stated that their proof followed the Spanish program. Their combative exchange with Buckmaster before the release seems to suggest that they believed as much. And they weren’t initially certain whether his work had been incorporated in their model’s training data.
paras.zh: 重要的是，也许是数学未来的预兆，专家们花了多长时间才意识到这一切。当 OpenAI 于 9 月 8 日公布其具有里程碑意义的成果时，公司官员明确多次表示，他们的证明遵循西班牙计划。他们在发布前与巴克马斯特的激烈交流似乎表明他们也相信这一点。他们最初不确定他的工作是否已纳入模型的训练数据中。

paras.en: That is, OpenAI didn’t understand its own model’s proof. And still, more than a month later, no one fully does.
paras.zh: 也就是说，OpenAI 不理解自己模型的证明。然而，一个多月过去了，仍然没有人完全做到这一点。

paras.en: Last week the company dumped some 400 more results on the community. In the pre-AI era, at least a dozen of those results could have merited any human mathematician a Fields Medal—math’s Nobel Prize. There already aren’t enough experts on Earth to keep pace with the onslaught, and there’s no sign that it’s slowing down.
paras.zh: 上周，该公司向社区发布了大约 400 条结果。在前人工智能时代，其中至少有十几个成果可以让任何人类数学家获得菲尔兹奖——数学界的诺贝尔奖。地球上已经没有足够的专家来跟上这场攻击的步伐，而且没有迹象表明它正在放缓。

articles.title: The mathematical secret behind why rose petals curl

paras.en: While they are undeniably beautiful, roses aren’t among my favorite flowers—too clichéd and romantic. I much prefer an indestructible cactus, a carnivorous plant or a hipster monstera, which, of course, is a must-have in any Japandi-style apartment. But after hearing about the research findings of physicist Eran Sharon’s lab at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, I’m reconsidering roses. From a mathematical perspective, the flowers are pretty cool—or at least their petals are.
paras.zh: 虽然玫瑰无可否认地美丽，但玫瑰并不是我最喜欢的花——太陈词滥调和浪漫了。我更喜欢坚不可摧的仙人掌、食肉植物或时髦的龟背竹，当然，它们是任何日式公寓的必备品。但在听说耶路撒冷希伯来大学物理学家埃兰·沙龙实验室的研究结果后，我正在重新考虑玫瑰。从数学的角度来看，这些花非常酷——或者至少它们的花瓣是。

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
paras.zh: 如果您喜欢这篇文章，请考虑通过订阅来支持我们屡获殊荣的新闻报道。通过购买订阅，您将有助于确保有关塑造当今世界的发现和想法的影响力故事的未来。

paras.en: You can find many videos online explaining that the arrangement of a plant’s petals is related to the golden ratio or the Fibonacci sequence, indicating a deep connection between botany and mathematics. The reason isn’t that nature has a particular affinity for mathematics. Rather the most sunlight reaches the petals when they form an angle with one another that is irrational, meaning its measurements cannot be expressed as the ratio of two integers. The irrationality ensures that no petal is directly above another.
paras.zh: 你可以在网上找到很多视频，解释植物花瓣的排列与黄金比例或斐波那契数列有关，这表明植物学和数学之间有很深的联系。原因并不是大自然对数学有特殊的亲和力。相反，当花瓣彼此形成不合理的角度时，最多的阳光就会到达花瓣，这意味着它的测量结果不能表示为两个整数的比率。这种非理性确保没有花瓣直接位于另一个花瓣之上。

paras.en: Such insights have fascinated mathematicians and physicists for decades, which is why they have taken a closer look at plant growth. How, for example, can the curly leaf shape of Lollo Rossa lettuce be explained? Why does a carrot bend when it’s cut lengthwise? Questions like these can be answered quite easily with a little math and physics. But the arrangement of rose blossoms has been a long-standing scientific puzzle.
paras.zh: 几十年来，这些见解一直让数学家和物理学家着迷，这就是他们仔细研究植物生长的原因。例如，如何解释 Lollo Rossa 生菜的卷曲叶子形状？为什么胡萝卜纵向切时会弯曲？通过一点数学和物理知识就可以很容易地回答这些问题。但玫瑰花的排列一直是一个长期存在的科学难题。

paras.en: The shape of a leaf is influenced by many different factors, such as the speed of growth, the material and the environment it grows in. For example, if the edge of a leaf grows faster than its center, this can lead to a curled or wavy shape—as with Lollo lettuce. With carrots, on the other hand, the opposite is the case: the inside of the vegetable grows faster than its outside, but because of its firm structure, it usually retains a straight shape. If you quarter the vegetable lengthwise, the structure is weakened, and the insides of the pieces will bend outwards, making visible the pressure that has existed inside the carrot.
paras.zh: 叶子的形状受到许多不同因素的影响，例如生长速度、材料和生长环境。例如，如果叶子的边缘比中心生长得快，就会导致叶子卷曲或波浪形，就像 Lollo 生菜一样。另一方面，胡萝卜的情况正好相反：蔬菜的内部比外部生长得快，但由于其结构坚固，通常保持笔直的形状。如果将蔬菜纵向切成四份，结构就会减弱，蔬菜块的内部会向外弯曲，使胡萝卜内部存在的压力可见。

paras.en: Rose petals, however, differ from other flower shapes. They are not simply wavy or curved but have almost triangular tips. Such irregular segments are distinct among flowers. And this raises questions: What distinguishes rose petals from the leaves, petals and shoots of other plants?
paras.zh: 然而，玫瑰花瓣与其他花朵形状不同。它们不仅仅是波浪形或弯曲的，而且具有几乎三角形的尖端。这种不规则的片段在花朵中是明显的。这就提出了一个问题：玫瑰花瓣与其他植物的叶子、花瓣和芽有何不同？

paras.en: To find out, Sharon and his team dissected rose petals, devised theoretical models, created computer simulations and conducted experiments with rubber surfaces. They discovered that the shape of rose petals has a completely different geometric cause than that of other plants.
paras.zh: 为了找到答案，莎伦和他的团队解剖了玫瑰花瓣，设计了理论模型，创建了计算机模拟，并用橡胶表面进行了实验。他们发现玫瑰花瓣的形状与其他植物的形状有着完全不同的几何原因。

paras.en: The curling of flower petals can be explained mathematically: because of their differing growth rates, petals “want” to curl, but this is prevented by external factors—such as the tissue not being elastic enough. It’s like trying to flatten the surface of a sphere onto a plane—it’s simply impossible. This “Gauss incompatibility” leads to mechanical stresses that produce virtually all flower shapes.
paras.zh: 花瓣的卷曲可以用数学来解释：由于它们的生长速度不同，花瓣“想要”卷曲，但这会受到外部因素的阻止，例如组织弹性不够。这就像试图将球体表面压平成平面一样——根本不可能。这种“高斯不相容性”会导致产生几乎所有花朵形状的机械应力。

paras.en: Gauss incompatibility can only explain smooth and periodic patterns, however, as Sharon and his team were aware. But the shape of rose petals is neither periodic nor smooth: there are isolated locations where a point is formed. To understand this, the researchers first cut the petals into fine strips—once along the horizontal axis and once along the vertical axis. The team’s aim was to visualize the mechanical pressure acting on the petals, similar to cutting carrots to reveal their internal pressure.
paras.zh: 然而，正如沙龙和他的团队意识到的那样，高斯不相容只能解释平滑和周期性的模式。但玫瑰花瓣的形状既不是周期性的，也不是平滑的：有一些孤立的位置形成一个点。为了理解这一点，研究人员首先将花瓣切成细条——一次沿着水平轴，一次沿着垂直轴。该团队的目标是可视化作用在花瓣上的机械压力，类似于切胡萝卜以揭示其内部压力。

paras.en: The longitudinal strips of the rose petals did indeed curl up, suggesting that the petal preferentially curves in this direction. When cut along the horizontal axis, however, the petal segments remained unchanged. This means a petal possesses a kind of conical structure, which is compatible with a flat geometry and therefore shouldn’t create any internal tension. After all, a flat sheet of paper can easily be rolled into a cone or a cylinder. A rose petal can, in principle, be laid flat on a surface; this confirms that Gauss incompatibility isn’t what causes the unusual shape of the petal. But what causes it then?
paras.zh: 玫瑰花瓣的纵向条确实卷曲起来，表明花瓣优先朝这个方向弯曲。然而，当沿水平轴切割时，花瓣片段保持不变。这意味着花瓣具有一种圆锥形结构，与平面几何形状兼容，因此不应产生任何内部张力。毕竟，一张平坦的纸可以很容易地卷成圆锥体或圆柱体。原则上，玫瑰花瓣可以平放在表面上；这证实了高斯不相容性并不是导致花瓣形状异常的原因。但到底是什么原因造成的呢？

paras.en: Similar questions are addressed in mechanics and industrial manufacturing processes because it’s crucial to know whether a manufactured component exhibits internal stresses and could break. Besides the Gauss equations, which must be considered, there are other equations at play: the Mainardi-Codazzi-Peterson equations. These state, among other things, that the normal vector (the vector perpendicular to the surface) must be uniquely defined. And as Sharon’s team discovered, this isn’t the case with rose petals. They therefore exhibit a geometric incompatibility, albeit a different one than that of other flowers.
paras.zh: 类似的问题在机械和工业制造过程中也得到解决，因为了解制造的部件是否表现出内应力并可能破裂至关重要。除了必须考虑的高斯方程之外，还有其他方程在起作用：Mainardi-Codazzi-Peterson 方程。除其他外，这些规定必须唯一定义法向矢量（垂直于表面的矢量）。正如莎伦的团队发现的那样，玫瑰花瓣的情况并非如此。因此，它们表现出几何上的不相容性，尽管与其他花不同。

paras.en: Imagine cutting a slice of a pie chart, a shape that roughly corresponds to a flower petal. Now the left side of the slice wants to curl up, and so does the right side—but in different ways. This creates a point in the circular segment where tension accumulates, which in turn leads to the formation of a pointed edge. This can even happen in several places, resulting in multiple points.
paras.zh: 想象一下切下饼图的一片，其形状大致对应于花瓣。现在切片的左侧想要卷曲，右侧也是如此，但方式不同。这会在圆弧段中产生一个张力累积的点，进而导致尖边的形成。这种情况甚至可能发生在多个地方，从而导致多个点。

paras.en: Sharon’s research group was able to confirm this mechanism, which had never been observed in nature otherwise, using computer simulations and experiments. Although the team cannot rule out the possibility of other natural processes exhibiting Mainardi-Codazzi-Peterson incompatibility, rose blossoms are currently the only known example.
paras.zh: 沙龙的研究小组通过计算机模拟和实验证实了这种在自然界中从未观察到的机制。尽管该团队不能排除其他自然过程表现出迈纳迪-科达齐-彼得森不相容性的可能性，但玫瑰花是目前唯一已知的例子。

paras.en: And that’s what makes roses so unique. I’m still not sure if that’s enough to convince me of their beauty. But I’d never previously considered why flowers look the way they do, so I acknowledge that roses add some new insights into mathematics—and therefore appreciate them a little more.
paras.zh: 这就是玫瑰如此独特的原因。我仍然不确定这是否足以让我相信它们的美丽。但我以前从未考虑过为什么花朵看起来像这样，所以我承认玫瑰为数学增添了一些新的见解，因此更加欣赏它们。

paras.en: And as physicist Richard Feynman pointed out in an interview in the early 1980s, looking at a flower with a scientist’s eyes raises “all kinds of interesting questions,” which, in his view, “only adds to the excitement, the mystery and the awe of a flower.”
paras.zh: 正如物理学家理查德·费曼 (Richard Feynman) 在 20 世纪 80 年代初的一次采访中指出的那样，用科学家的眼睛观察一朵花会引发“各种有趣的问题”，在他看来，这“只会增加对花的兴奋、神秘和敬畏。”

paras.en: This article originally appeared in Spektrum der Wissenschaft and was reproduced with permission. It was translated from the original German version with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by our editors.
paras.zh: 本文最初发表于 Spektrum der Wissenschaft 并经许可转载。它是在人工智能的帮助下从德语原文翻译而来，并由我们的编辑审阅。

articles.title: What happens when you lose your voice?
articles.author: Laura Sanders

paras.en: A voice matters not just to the person who is speaking, but to the people listening, too. A study on moms and their daughters demonstrates the power of a voice by showing that moms’ voices reduced a measure of stress in the daughters. The same wasn’t true for texting.
paras.zh: 声音不仅对说话的人很重要，对听的人也很重要。一项针对母亲和女儿的研究表明，母亲的声音可以减轻女儿们的压力，从而证明了声音的力量。对于短信来说情况并非如此。

paras.en: In the second episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, you’ll hear more about the ripple effects created by a lost voice. Jules Rodriguez says that as his voice slipped away, it felt like he was fading. But could a new, more realistic digital voice step in and change his story?
paras.zh: 在《深渊：跟我说话》的第二集中，您将听到更多关于失声所产生的连锁反应。朱尔斯·罗德里格斯说，当他的声音消失时，他感觉自己正在消失。但一个新的、更真实的数字声音能否介入并改变他的故事呢？

paras.en: Hear about a tough medical decision Jules and his family were facing, and whether a sophisticated voice clone could influence his choice.
paras.zh: 了解朱尔斯和他的家人面临的艰难医疗决定，以及复杂的声音克隆是否会影响他的选择。

paras.en: [reporter audio] Hi, this is Laura calling. This is Laura Sanders from Science News. Is now an OK time to talk about your paper coming out? I would love to start with just the very big picture question of why you did this study. Why did you do this study? What were you hoping to find?
paras.zh: [记者音频] 大家好，我是劳拉。我是《科学新闻》的劳拉·桑德斯。现在是谈论你的论文发表的好时机吗？我很想从一个非常宏观的问题开始，即你为什么要做这项研究。你为什么做这项研究？您希望找到什么？

paras.en: Laura Sanders: I’m a neuroscience reporter with Science News, which means I spend a lot of time reading research papers about the brain. One of my very favorite scientific papers, and there are a lot of them, so this is really saying something, is a study published way back in 2012.
paras.zh: 劳拉·桑德斯：我是《科学新闻》的神经科学记者，这意味着我花了很多时间阅读有关大脑的研究论文。我最喜欢的科学论文之一是 2012 年发表的一项研究，这样的论文有很多，所以这确实说明了一些事情。

paras.en: [voice] Researchers at the University of Wisconsin have found the sound of a mother’s voice triggers a physical response.
paras.zh: [声音]威斯康星大学的研究人员发现母亲的声音会引发身体反应。

paras.en: Sanders: Sixty-eight girls, all between the ages of 7 and 12, came into a lab in Madison, Wisconsin. For the experiment, these girls were asked to tell a story out loud and then perform a tricky subtraction problem in their heads. The whole time, they were being watched and evaluated by the researchers. I get sweaty just thinking about it. OK, so after that ordeal, the girls were separated into groups. Some girls got to see their moms in person and talk with them after their stressful performance. Some got to talk to their moms on the phone. Some got to text with their moms. And some just had to sit alone wondering what had just happened to them.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：68 名年龄在 7 岁到 12 岁之间的女孩来到威斯康星州麦迪逊市的一个实验室。在实验中，这些女孩被要求大声讲一个故事，然后在脑海中执行一个棘手的减法问题。整个过程中，研究人员一直在观察和评估它们。我光是想想就出汗。好吧，在那次磨难之后，女孩们被分成了几组。一些女孩在紧张的表演后可以亲自见到她们的妈妈并与她们交谈。有些人必须通过电话与妈妈交谈。有些人必须与妈妈发短信。有些人只能独自坐着，想知道自己刚刚发生了什么事。

paras.en: Later on, when researchers measured stress hormones in the girls, they found something startling. The girls who had talked to their moms, either in person or on the phone, had lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol than the girls who had just texted or had no contact.
paras.zh: 后来，当研究人员测量这些女孩的压力荷尔蒙时，他们发现了一些令人吃惊的事情。与妈妈面对面或通过电话交谈的女孩，其压力荷尔蒙皮质醇水平低于刚刚发短信或没有联系的女孩。

paras.en: The authors conclude that there’s something especially soothing about hearing a mom’s voice, some alchemy of familiar and calming sounds that a daughter’s brain wants to hear.
paras.zh: 作者得出的结论是，听到妈妈的声音有一种特别舒缓的感觉，女儿的大脑想听到一些熟悉而平静的声音。

paras.en: [voices] So call your mother. Good advice at any time.
paras.zh: [声音]所以给你妈妈打电话。随时提出好的建议。

paras.en: Sanders: In a full circle sort of way, I tell my own mom about the study after calling her to complain about a bunch of stuff.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：以一种完整的方式，我在打电话给我妈妈抱怨一堆事情后告诉她这项研究。

paras.en: [phone call] The talking mattered. The texting did nothing. The phone call and the in-person lowered their cortisol levels. Well good. So, the voice. That’s what you just did for me. That’s the deal. Well I’m glad. That’s just excellent. Thanks, Mom. All right. Yeah, talk to you later. Bye. Bye.
paras.zh: [电话] 谈话很重要。发短信什么也没做。电话和面对面的交流降低了他们的皮质醇水平。好极了。那么，声音。这就是你刚刚为我做的。就是这样。嗯，我很高兴。那真是太棒了。谢谢，妈妈。好的。是的，稍后再聊。再见。再见。

paras.en: Kate Nilson: And, you know, it’s so funny. Every time I’m with my parents, I think I need to record their voices. How can I be in this world and not have their voices recorded? So I need to get on that.
paras.zh: 凯特·尼尔森：而且，你知道，这太有趣了。每次和父母在一起的时候，我想我都需要录下他们的声音。我来到这个世界怎么可能没有他们的声音呢？所以我需要继续下去。

paras.en: Sanders: That’s speech-language pathologist Kate Nilson, a person very familiar with the specialness of voices.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：那是言语病理学家凯特·尼尔森，她非常熟悉声音的特殊性。

paras.en: Nilson: Just for all the reasons we just talked about, right? So when I get stressed out, I can just listen to my own mom’s voice. I mean, I’m in my 40s and I still need my mom, so.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：就因为我们刚才谈到的所有原因，对吧？所以当我感到压力的时候，我可以听听妈妈的声音。我的意思是，我已经 40 多岁了，但我仍然需要妈妈，所以。

paras.en: Sanders: I mean, yes, listen to the nice comforting sounds my mom makes on the phone when I go through my laundry list of problems.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：我的意思是，是的，当我列出一长串问题时，听听我妈妈在电话里发出的美妙的安慰声音。

paras.en: [phone call] Yeah. I hear it in your voice. Oh, that’s sad. Get me some phone numbers and I’ll make calls. That’s pretty intensive stuff.
paras.zh: [电话] 是的。我从你的声音里听到了。哦，那很伤心。给我一些电话号码，我会打电话。这是相当密集的事情。

paras.en: [intro] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi! Your voice is you.
paras.zh: [简介] 嘿妈妈，我可以告诉你一件事吗？声音绝对是您身份的一个组成部分。你想说话吗？那增加的一层就是你。你好？你的声音。你好！你的声音就是你。

paras.en: Sanders: This desire to capture voices that have special meaning to us, to hold them close, is a perspective I heard over and over. That’s because voices don’t just mean something to the people who make them. Voices mean just as much to the people hearing them.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这种渴望捕捉对我们有特殊意义的声音，将它们紧紧地抓住，是我一遍又一遍听到的观点。这是因为声音不仅仅对声音的制作者有意义。声音对于听到声音的人来说同样重要。

paras.en: Welcome to this second episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me, from Science News. I’m Laura Sanders, and today we’re going to explore what it means to lose the ability to talk.
paras.zh: 欢迎收看《科学新闻》的《深渊》第二集《跟我说话》。我是劳拉·桑德斯，今天我们将探讨失去说话能力意味着什么。

paras.en: Sanders: Jules Rodriguez has a unique perspective on the human voice.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：朱尔斯·罗德里格斯对人类声音有着独特的看法。

paras.en: Jules: Your voice is different because it’s a big part of your identity. I knew early on, my voice may disappear, so we made sure to record it while I still had it.
paras.zh: 朱尔斯：你的声音与众不同，因为它是你身份的重要组成部分。我很早就知道，我的声音可能会消失，所以我们一定要趁我还有声音的时候把它录下来。

paras.en: Sanders: Jules is a podcaster, former science teacher, comedian, husband, and dad who lives in Miami. He was diagnosed with ALS in 2020. The progressive nature of the disease means that people start losing strength and the ability to move, all while their brains and cognition are unaffected. That loss includes the muscles that are required to talk.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：朱尔斯是一名播客、前科学老师、喜剧演员、丈夫和父亲，住在迈阿密。他于 2020 年被诊断出患有 ALS。这种疾病的进行性意味着人们开始失去力量和移动能力，但他们的大脑和认知不受影响。这种损失包括说话所需的肌肉。

paras.en: MA: I still remember the first time. This was in 2022, the summer of ‘22, that I heard the first little crack in his voice that let me know something’s changing.
paras.zh: MA：我还记得第一次的情景。那是在 2022 年，也就是 22 年的夏天，我第一次听到他声音里的细微声音，让我知道有些事情正在发生变化。

paras.en: Sanders: That’s Jules’ wife, MA. When I was first connected to Jules and MA, I learned they had a podcast called The Couple Shift.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：那是朱尔斯的妻子，MA。当我第一次联系到 Jules 和 MA 时，我得知他们有一个名为“The Couple Shift”的播客。

paras.en: [podcast]: Well, hello there, everyone. Welcome to episode zero of our brand new podcast.
paras.zh: 【播客】：大家好。欢迎来到我们全新播客的第 0 集。

paras.en: Sanders: About their marriage and themselves as they dealt with life, careers and family. I started listening at the beginning.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：关于他们的婚姻以及他们自己在处理生活、事业和家庭时的情况。我一开始就开始听。

paras.en: [podcast] My name is Maria Aleandra. I am a life and business coach, and this is my amazing hubby. Julian Tomas. And I’m a former teacher and amazing husband. He sure is.
paras.zh: [播客] 我的名字是玛丽亚·阿莉安德拉。我是一名生活和商业教练，这是我了不起的丈夫。朱利安·托马斯.我以前是一名教师，也是一位出色的丈夫。他确实是。

paras.en: Sanders: They were so sweet with each other. Playful, teasing, funny, yet sincere and loving. Listen to them being cute.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：他们彼此非常甜蜜。俏皮、戏弄、有趣，但又真诚又充满爱心。听他们说的很可爱。

paras.en: [podcast] So I got frustrated. And by lash shout, it’s like an outburst. It’s a [beep] what the hell? You know, that kind of deal. Do we have to bleep out? We do. Yes. Sorry. Gosh darn it. I should know better. Is that what you’re going to tell me? Yeah, that’s what my look is saying right now.
paras.zh: [播客]所以我很沮丧。猛烈的喊叫，就像爆发一样。这是[嘟嘟]什么鬼？你知道，就是这样的交易。我们必须发出哔哔声吗？我们做到了。是的。对不起。天哪，该死。我应该更了解。这就是你要告诉我的吗？是的，这就是我现在的样子。

paras.en: Sanders: They started recording their podcast in 2019, before Jules’ ALS diagnosis. As I listened, moving from early episodes to later ones, I got this feeling of time zooming past, just so fast I couldn’t catch it.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：他们从 2019 年开始录制播客，当时朱尔斯被诊断出 ALS。当我听的时候，从前几集转到后来的几集，我有一种时间飞逝的感觉，快得我都跟不上。

paras.en: [podcast] We went to go see the doctor again to get his final assessment, I guess.
paras.zh: [播客]我想我们又去看了医生以获得他的最终评估。

paras.en: Sanders: Unlike the Jules and MA from early episodes, I already knew the twist, the gut punch of what was coming.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：与早期剧集中的朱尔斯和马不同，我已经知道即将发生的事情的转折和冲击。

paras.en: [podcast] Unfortunately, the news is that he believes it’s ALS or SMA, which is spinal muscular atrophy. It was a really hard hit in the balls. And it’s been a very difficult couple weeks.
paras.zh: [播客] 不幸的是，有消息称他认为这是 ALS 或 SMA，即脊髓性肌萎缩症。这真是一次重击。这是非常困难的几周。

paras.en: Sanders: As I moved through the episodes, I started hearing a difference in Jules’ voice. His voice got slower, weaker, fuzzier. I asked him recently what that was like.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：当我观看这些剧集时，我开始听到朱尔斯的声音有所不同。他的声音越来越慢、越来越弱、越来越模糊。我最近问他那是什么样的。

paras.en: Jules: It’s strange with the podcast because you can hear my real voice slowly decay till we stop.
paras.zh: 朱尔斯：播客很奇怪，因为你可以听到我真实的声音慢慢衰减，直到我们停止。

paras.en: MA: Yeah. It’s really this archive of what he sounded like, little by little as it changed. And it was, yeah, like very disarming to get to that moment. And then you begin to get used to it and you sort of work around it and appreciate that it’s still there. Yeah, that was really, really difficult for me.
paras.zh: 马：是的。这实际上是他听起来的档案，一点一点地改变。是的，那一刻让人非常放松。然后你开始习惯它，你会解决它并欣赏它仍然存在。是的，这对我来说真的非常困难。

paras.en: Sanders: Jules and MA even talk about this very process on their podcast, of having a record of their voices through time. Here’s a clip from 2024 when Jules could still talk, but with difficulty.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：朱尔斯和马云甚至在他们的播客上谈论了这个过程，记录了他们随时间变化的声音。这是 2024 年的一个片段，当时朱尔斯仍然可以说话，但很困难。

paras.en: [podcast] To me, it’s so weird. Yes. We’re such different people and different mindsets and just different, well, lack of experience and dealing with all this. It’s so freaking beautiful, though, because you can see the whole evolution of us. It’s a living legacy of a life lived. A living legacy. A living legacy of a life lived. You and your words. Me and my words.
paras.zh: [播客]对我来说，这太奇怪了。是的。我们是不同的人，有着不同的心态，只是不同，缺乏处理这一切的经验。不过，它是如此美丽，因为你可以看到我们的整个进化过程。这是一个活生生的生活遗产。活生生的遗产。一个活生生的活生生的遗产。你和你的话。我和我的话。

paras.en: Sanders: In those last episodes, I was hearing the change in Jules’s voice. I was also hearing his emotions. I was hearing his weariness. Jules compares the process of losing his voice to a Back to the Future moment that any person raised in the 80s will remember. It’s when Marty sees a photograph of his family in a timeline that no longer exists.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：在最后几集中，我听到朱尔斯声音的变化。我也听到了他的情绪。我听到了他的疲倦。朱尔斯将失声的过程比作任何在 80 年代长大的人都会记得的回到未来的时刻。当马蒂在一条不再存在的时间线上看到他家人的照片时。

paras.en: [movie audio] Just as I thought. This proves my theory. Look at your brother. His head’s gone. It’s like he’s been erased.
paras.zh: [电影音频] 和我想的一样。这证明了我的理论。看看你的兄弟。他的头不见了。他就像被抹去了一样。

paras.en: Jules: For me, it felt like I was fading away. Like when Marty McFly was seeing his family fade away in the picture he had in Back to the Future.
paras.zh: 朱尔斯：对我来说，感觉就像我正在消失。就像马蒂·麦克弗莱在《回到未来》的照片中看到他的家人逐渐消失一样。

paras.en: Sanders: A piece of Jules was fading away. A really important piece that tells other people something about his internal state, his emotions, where he’s been, and what’s happening now.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：朱尔斯的一部分正在消失。这是一个非常重要的作品，它告诉其他人一些关于他的内心状态、他的情绪、他去过哪里以及现在正在发生的事情。

paras.en: Voices are packed with all sorts of signals. Sometimes they’re a little bit unexpected, like when a guy you don’t know all that well says “about” and you realize he is Canadian. Sometimes they’re absolutely obvious, like a strong Southern drawl. Voices can signal energy levels, whether your allergies are acting up, where you were born, and how old you are. Here’s Greg Bryant of UCLA.
paras.zh: 声音中充满了各种各样的信号。有时他们有点出乎意料，比如当一个你不太了解的人说“关于”时，你意识到他是加拿大人。有时它们是绝对明显的，就像浓重的南方拖腔。声音可以表明你的能量水平、你是否过敏、你出生在哪里以及你的年龄。这是加州大学洛杉矶分校的格雷格·布莱恩特的报道。

paras.en: Bryant: Cues are any kind of property that might predict something about the sender. You can tell, for example, how big a person is by hearing their voice. You can tell if they’re male or female generally by hearing their voice. You can tell if they’re old or young, right? So there’s all these kind of basic properties of a person that are indexed in a voice.
paras.zh: 布莱恩特：线索是任何可以预测发送者某些信息的属性。例如，您可以通过听声音来判断一个人有多大。一般通过听声音就可以判断他们是男性还是女性。你能看出他们是老是年轻，对吧？因此，一个人的所有这些基本属性都可以在声音中索引。

paras.en: Sanders: Voices can carry emotions too. A smile, for example, has subtle sound cues.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：声音也可以承载情感。例如，微笑就有微妙的声音提示。

paras.en: Bryant: There’s a slight increase in pitch when you smile and then you change what are called formants. The formants are structures in the speech signal underlying what your perception of vowels is. They’re energy bands that are associated with resonating chambers in your throat and in your mouth. And so when you are moving your tongue around and changing your lips and doing other things going, ahowowowow, you’re changing the formants. That’s the resonating bands of energy in the voice. So when you smile, then the formants change a little bit. And it’s detectable. It’s subtle, but you can hear it for sure.
paras.zh: Bryant: There’s a slight increase in pitch when you smile and then you change what are called formants. The formants are structures in the speech signal underlying what your perception of vowels is. They’re energy bands that are associated with resonating chambers in your throat and in your mouth. And so when you are moving your tongue around and changing your lips and doing other things going, ahowowowow, you’re changing the formants. That’s the resonating bands of energy in the voice. So when you smile, then the formants change a little bit.而且它是可以检测到的。虽然很微妙，但你肯定能听到。

paras.en: Sanders: See if you can detect it here. It’s Jules introducing an episode of their podcast in 2020.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：看看你能不能在这里发现它。这是Jules在2020年推出的一集播客。

paras.en: [podcast] So my wife comes to me today, and she says, babe, I have diarrhea.
paras.zh: [播客] 所以我的妻子今天来找我，她说，宝贝，我腹泻了。

paras.en: Sanders: So setting aside the content he chose to share, which was a bold choice, you can hear the grin in his voice.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：所以抛开他选择分享的内容（这是一个大胆的选择），你可以听到他声音中的笑容。

paras.en: [podcast] Before we get into that, though, I also want to say one quick thing. Happy birthday, my love.
paras.zh: [播客] 不过，在我们开始讨论之前，我还想快速说一件事。生日快乐，我的爱人。

paras.en: Sanders: That’s because his smile pulled his lips slightly upward and changed the shape of the air coming out, thereby changing the sound of his voice. All of these signals in the voice exist because voices are made by bodies. Bodies that move, smile, change, grow older, get sick. Our voices are actually a stunningly sophisticated bit of biology.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：那是因为他的微笑将嘴唇稍微向上拉，改变了空气的形状，从而改变了他的声音。声音中的所有这些信号之所以存在，是因为声音是由身体发出的。身体会移动、微笑、变化、变老、生病。我们的声音实际上是生物学中极其复杂的一部分。

paras.en: Jessica Pietrowski: You think about how, you know, we’re just talking, we’re just voicing, we’re barely even thinking about what we’re doing, but actually upwards close to a hundred muscles are being used.
paras.zh: 杰西卡·皮特罗斯基：你想想，你知道，我们只是在说话，我们只是在发声，我们几乎没有想到我们在做什么，但实际上有近一百块肌肉正在被使用。

paras.en: Sanders: That’s speech-language pathologist and scientist Jessica Pietrowski of UC Davis.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这是加州大学戴维斯分校的言语病理学家和科学家杰西卡·皮特罗斯基。

paras.en: Pietrowski: When we go to voice, we have to take a breath. Breath comes up, the diaphragm is contracting to get that breath. Breath comes up below the vocal folds, these tissues here, vibrates the vocal folds, creates a tone. That tone comes up through the oral cavity and other spaces, and resonates. And then you have to articulate it, and, and make the sounds clear and sharp. And then you have speech. And so really, you know, we’re not thinking about this as we’re doing it, but it’s incredibly complex and intricate and really an incredible human feat.
paras.zh: Pietrowski：当我们使用声音时，我们必须喘口气。呼吸上升，横膈膜收缩以呼吸。呼吸从声带下方上升，这些组织振动声带，产生音调。这种音调通过口腔和其他空间传出，并产生共鸣。然后你必须清晰地表达出来，并且让声音清晰锐利。然后你就可以讲话了。所以说真的，你知道，我们在做这件事的时候并没有考虑到这一点，但它是极其复杂和错综复杂的，确实是一项令人难以置信的人类壮举。

paras.en: Sanders: Right now, as I say these words to you, I’m pushing air out of my body and using my muscles to move my diaphragm, face, throat, and mouth to make tiny ripples of sound shaped with a precision far below the level of my conscious perception. This mechanical, biological, physical feat is what allows me to shape air into sounds that then move to your ears.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：现在，当我对你说这些话时，我正在将空气从体内推出，并用我的肌肉移动我的隔膜、面部、喉咙和嘴巴，以远远低于我意识感知水平的精度形成微小的声音涟漪。这种机械、生物、物理的壮举使我能够将空气塑造成声音，然后传送到你的耳朵。

paras.en: Sergey Stavisky: So this is a very engineering-y perspective, but one thing about voices, it is our fastest means to communicate what we’re thinking.
paras.zh: 谢尔盖·斯塔维斯基：所以这是一个非常工程化的视角，但关于声音的一件事是，它是我们传达我们想法的最快方式。

paras.en: Sanders: Sergey Stavisky co-directs the UC Davis Neuroprosthetics Lab, focused on using technology to replace or repair parts of the damaged nervous system.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：谢尔盖·斯塔维斯基（Sergey Stavisky）是加州大学戴维斯分校神经假体实验室的共同负责人，该实验室专注于使用技术来替换或修复受损神经系统的部分。

paras.en: Stavisky: So it’s actually, if you step back, kind of magical. So you have some idea in your mind, and your brain is able to take that idea, form it into language. So that’s already a complicated step. And then it’s able to move almost a hundred muscles in your tongue, in your jaw, and in your larynx to vibrate air in this exquisitely precise way.
paras.zh: 斯塔维斯基：所以，如果你退一步看，这实际上有点神奇。所以你脑子里有一些想法，你的大脑能够接受这个想法，将其转化为语言。所以这已经是一个复杂的步骤了。然后它能够​​移动你舌头、下巴和喉部的近一百块肌肉，以这种极其精确的方式振动空气。

paras.en: Sanders: But then, even more magic happens when those vibrations move into someone else’s ear.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：但是，当这些振动进入别人的耳朵时，更多的魔力就会发生。

paras.en: Stavisky: Those vibrations are going to fly through the air and they’re going to hit someone else’s eardrum and it’s going to vibrate that, and it’s going to vibrate the hair cells. And it’s going to send a bunch of nerve signals to their brain and they’re going to first make sense of the sounds you’re making amidst all of the other sounds, whether there’s background conversation or a train rumbling by or a dog barking. But then beyond that, they’re going to not just hear the words you just said, but remember all the previous words, put them together and like get the same idea in their brain. I mean, it’s telepathy through mechanical means.
paras.zh: 斯塔维斯基：这些振动会在空气中飞翔，它们会撞击别人的耳膜，耳膜会振动，毛细胞也会振动。它将向他们的大脑发送一堆神经信号，他们将首先理解你在所有其他声音中发出的声音，无论是背景对话、火车隆隆驶过还是狗吠。但除此之外，他们不仅会听到你刚才说的话，还会记住之前的所有单词，将它们放在一起，就像在他们的大脑中得到相同的想法。我的意思是，这是通过机械手段进行心灵感应。

paras.en: Sanders: Telepathy through mechanical means. When you step back and think about it, it’s an absolute marvel. So here I am floating these ripples out toward my microphone. And then through more technology, they are reaching you, where your own amazing machinery senses those ripples and turns them into meaning. So with these ripples, I’m putting something into your mind.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：通过机械手段进行心灵感应。当你退后一步思考时，这绝对是一个奇迹。所以我在这里将这些涟漪飘向我的麦克风。然后通过更多的技术，它们会到达你身边，你自己神奇的机器会感知到这些涟漪并将其转化为意义。因此，通过这些涟漪，我将一些东西放入你的脑海中。

paras.en: Stavisky: We have this like shared scaffolding of understanding where I can pretty much visualize anything I want and with enough words, make someone else put that into their mind. And I think that’s a really remarkable ability. And that’s like the basis of civilization and learning and science and connection.
paras.zh: 斯塔维斯基：我们有一个共享的理解框架，我几乎可以想象我想要的任何东西，并用足够的语言让其他人将其放入他们的脑海中。我认为这是一种非常了不起的能力。这就像文明、学习、科学和联系的基础。

paras.en: Sanders: But there’s something happening before all of this muscle moving and air rippling, and it’s something that Stavisky just mentioned. My words first started taking shape somewhere else. They started in my brain. Certain clusters of my synapses fired as I thought about what to say. This intricate path from brain to muscles to sculpted air is behind every word we say.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：但是在所有这些肌肉移动和空气波动之前发生了一些事情，这就是斯塔维斯基刚才提到的。我的话首先在其他地方开始成形。它们开始在我的脑海里。当我思考该说什么时，我的某些突触簇会放电。我们所说的每一个字背后都有这条从大脑到肌肉再到雕刻空气的复杂路径。

paras.en: Casey Harrell: Hello there and thanks for being patient with me as I was running a bit late.
paras.zh: 凯西·哈勒尔：您好，感谢您对我的耐心，因为我有点晚了。

paras.en: Sanders: When I met Casey Harrell on Zoom, I asked him to tell me a little bit about himself.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：当我在 Zoom 上见到凯西·哈雷尔时，我请他告诉我一些关于他自己的事情。

paras.en: Casey: That is both the easiest and the hardest question to answer, right? So my name is Casey Harrell, and I am 47 years old. I grew up in the Atlanta area and have lived in the Bay Area for the past 23 years, most of them with my wife, Levana, and our seven-year-old daughter, who is going on 17. I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it.
paras.zh: 凯西：这是最简单也是最难回答的问题，对吧？我叫凯西·哈勒尔，今年 47 岁。 I grew up in the Atlanta area and have lived in the Bay Area for the past 23 years, most of them with my wife, Levana, and our seven-year-old daughter, who is going on 17. I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it.

paras.en: Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has taken a lot from him. He can no longer move most of his body. That includes speech muscles.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：像朱尔斯一样，凯西也患有肌萎缩侧索硬化症。疾病夺去了他的很多生命。他的大部分身体已经无法移动。这包括言语肌肉。

paras.en: Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020.
paras.zh: 凯西：2020 年确诊后不久，我就开始失去说话的能力。

paras.en: Sanders: With time, he could no longer talk clearly enough to be understood.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：随着时间的推移，他的讲话不再清晰到让人理解。

paras.en: Casey: Then it became a slow-motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.
paras.zh: 凯西：然后它变成了一场多年的慢动作车祸，直到几乎没有人能够理解我。其他一些经常在附近的朋友应该能够理解我在说什么。我基本上依靠我的助手​​和我的妻子充当我向其他人提供翻译的工作。我没有去任何地方，甚至在没有他们的情况下进行视频通话，无论是其中一个还是两个。

paras.en: Sanders: Casey’s life in the Bay Area was changing in difficult, almost impossible ways. Like Jules, Casey had received an ALS diagnosis in 2020. Like Jules, he had a kid, a partner, a career, a big, full life. And then wham, life threw them one of the biggest curveballs you can imagine. These two men, separated by 3,000 miles, Jules in Miami, Casey in Oakland, were both facing big losses. And one of the biggest of all was their ability to talk.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：凯西在湾区的生活正在以艰难、几乎不可能的方式发生变化。和朱尔斯一样，凯西在 2020 年被诊断出肌萎缩侧索硬化症。和朱尔斯一样，他也有一个孩子、一个伴侣、一份事业、一个充实而充实的生活。然后砰的一声，生活给了他们一个你能想象到的最大的曲线球。这两个人相距 3,000 英里，朱尔斯在迈阿密，凯西在奥克兰，都面临着巨大的损失。其中最重要的一点就是他们的说话能力。

paras.en: Speech-language pathologist Kate Nilson walks me through some of the standard approaches that she uses when she’s working with people who face similar futures. There’s a process called voice banking.
paras.zh: 言语病理学家凯特·尼尔森向我介绍了她在与面临相似未来的人一起工作时使用的一些标准方法。有一个称为语音银行的流程。

paras.en: Nilson: So voice banking is the idea of recording specific sentences that you might not actually say in real life, but predetermined sentences that you record that give the software the combinations of sounds that it needs to make a computer voice that sounds like you.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：因此，语音银行的想法是记录您在现实生活中实际上可能不会说的特定句子，而是记录您录制的预定句子，这些句子为软件提供了发出听起来像您的计算机声音所需的声音组合。

paras.en: Sanders: That process has actually improved quite a bit in recent years.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：近年来，这个过程实际上有了很大改进。

paras.en: Nilson: When I started doing this, it was 1600 sentences. Now it can be an app on your phone that you do at home. It can be a website that you go to. The software that I use most of the time is 50 sentences. It can be done in like 15 minutes. It’s really come a long way and the voices are pretty darn amazing in how how true to the person they are. But they are still a computerized voice, right? They’re they’re they’re taking combinations of sounds and splicing them together. So it sounds computerized.
paras.zh: Nilson：当我开始这样做时，有 1600 个句子。现在它可以是您在家中使用的手机应用程序。它可以是您访问的网站。我最常使用的软件是50句。大约 15 分钟内即可完成。这确实已经取得了很大的进步，而且这些声音对于他们的真实性来说是非常惊人的。但它们仍然是计算机化的声音，对吗？他们正在将声音组合起来并将它们拼接在一起。所以听起来是电脑化的。

paras.en: Sanders: Voice banking has the benefit of being flexible. This voice can say anything a person wants, but it sounds off. There’s another approach. This one’s called message banking.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：语音银行的优点是灵活。这个声音可以说任何人想说的话，但听起来不太对劲。还有另一种方法。这就是所谓的消息银行。

paras.en: Nilson: So the idea of message banking is we just record an entire message. So instead of using that computer voice to say, “Good night, honey, I love you,” we can just record someone saying, “Good night, honey, I love you,” with their voice, like, with their true inflection and meaning.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：所以消息银行的想法是我们只记录整个消息。因此，我们不必用计算机的声音说“晚安，亲爱的，我爱你”，而是可以录制某人说的“晚安，亲爱的，我爱你”，用他们的声音，就像他们真正的语调和含义一样。

paras.en: Sanders: The beauty of these messages is that they capture the quirks of a person’s voice.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这些信息的美妙之处在于它们捕捉到了一个人声音的怪癖。

paras.en: Nilson: You know, I live in Minnesota, and so there’s a lot of ooftas and doncha knows, and those kinds of things that do not come out right when you type them into a computer.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：你知道，我住在明尼苏达州，所以有很多 ooftas 和 doncha 知道的东西，当你把它们输入电脑时，这些东西不会正确显示。

paras.en: Sanders: Nilson encounters these sorts of sounds when she’s helping people save recordings of their voice for the future.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：尼尔森在帮助人们保存自己的声音录音以供将来使用时遇到了这类声音。

paras.en: Nilson: You gotta get all those right sayings with the right, you know, “o’s” in them.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：你必须让所有这些正确的说法都带有正确的“o”。

paras.en: Sanders: These recorded messages are often things like an inside joke with the exact right timing or a favorite little nickname for someone special.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这些录制的信息通常是恰逢其时的内部笑话，或者是给某个特别的人最喜欢的小绰号。

paras.en: Nilson: It can be really emotional. And that’s, when you’re recording the sentences that are predetermined and they’re not sentences that you would normally say, that can be easy. But when your family has written down a list of meaningful words that they want to hear in your voice and you know that you’re recording it because you might lose your voice, that can be really emotional. And it can be hard. And I fully understand that, but we can also have fun with it.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：这可能真的很情绪化。也就是说，当您录制预先确定的句子并且它们不是您通常会说的句子时，这可能很容易。但是，当您的家人写下一系列他们希望在您的声音中听到的有意义的单词，并且您知道您录制它是因为您可能会失去声音时，这可能会非常情绪化。这可能很难。我完全理解这一点，但我们也可以从中获得乐趣。

paras.en: Sanders: Pre-recorded jokes come up pretty often when people are choosing what messages to preserve for later use. And swear words come up surprisingly often too, Nilson tells me.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：当人们选择保留哪些消息以供以后使用时，经常会出现预先录制的笑话。尼尔森告诉我，脏话也经常出现，令人惊讶。

paras.en: Nilson: I had someone come in just the other day, and they had an entire category of recorded cuss words. So that’s important. Well, right? I mean, you don’t want them to be monotone when you’re frustrated. You want the right emphasis to come out on that.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：前几天有人进来，他们录下了一大堆脏话。所以这很重要。嗯，对吧？我的意思是，当你感到沮丧时，你不希望它们变得单调。你希望对此有正确的强调。

paras.en: Sanders: It takes the sails out of it for sure if it’s monotone.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：如果它是单调的，那么它肯定会变得毫无意义。

paras.en: Nilson: Yeah, exactly. I mean, that’s communication, right? That’s important communication. So I guess it doesn’t really surprise me anymore, but it’s fun nonetheless.
paras.zh: 尼尔森：是的，完全正确。我的意思是，这就是沟通，对吗？这是重要的沟通。所以我想这不再让我感到惊讶，但仍然很有趣。

paras.en: Sanders: She says some people come to her with entire folders of swears, folders that she refused to share with me for the story, by the way.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：她说有些人带着一整套脏话来找她，顺便说一句，她拒绝与我分享这些文件夹。

paras.en: Nilson: The best part is it was a swear folder with all these different swear words and like different sayings and whatever. And then just one of them had a call-out to a specific person. And I was like, what did that person do to you that he’s the only one that has a specific? And then he laughed and he typed out, “If you knew him, you’d understand.”
paras.zh: 尼尔森：最好的部分是它是一个脏话文件夹，里面有所有这些不同的脏话，比如不同的谚语等等。然后其中只有一个人向特定的人发出了呼唤。我当时想，那个人对你做了什么，他是唯一一个有具体行动的人？然后他笑了，打字道：“如果你认识他，你就会明白。”

paras.en: Sanders: All of these quirks, the swears, the smiles in the voice, the familiar jokes, all of these things make a particular voice special. Jules created a banked voice. He didn’t love the result.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：所有这些怪癖、脏话、声音中的微笑、熟悉的笑话，所有这些都让特定的声音变得特别。朱尔斯发出了沉闷的声音。他不喜欢这个结果。

paras.en: Jules: What I learned from banking my voice was that it really wasn’t my voice. It was more like a robot trying to emulate my voice. It had no emotion or tone behind it.
paras.zh: 朱尔斯：我从存储我的声音中学到的是，这实际上不是我的声音。它更像是一个试图模仿我声音的机器人。它背后没有任何情感或语气。

paras.en: Sanders: This was a problem because it got in the way of something Jules wanted to do. The turmoil of ALS forced some clarity for him about what he wanted out of life, what he wanted to spend his time doing. And one of those answers, it turns out, was comedy. After his diagnosis, while he still had his voice, he performed stand-up a few times.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这是一个问题，因为它妨碍了朱尔斯想做的事情。 ALS 的混乱迫使他清楚地认识到自己想要从生活中得到什么，想要把时间花在做什么上。事实证明，这些答案之一就是喜剧。确诊后，他在还能说话的情况下表演了几次单口相声。

paras.en: Sanders: But as his voice got harder to use, things changed. Jules could still talk, but it took a lot of work, especially since he was often using a mask for extra oxygen.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：但随着他的声音变得越来越难用，情况发生了变化。朱尔斯仍然可以说话，但这需要做很多工作，特别是因为他经常使用面罩获取额外的氧气。

paras.en: MA: He was wearing the mask pretty much the entire time. So his voice was very labored, because you have to take the breath in to utter anything. So it was very choppy. But he did have a voice.
paras.zh: MA：他几乎一直戴着面具。所以他的声音非常吃力，因为你必须屏住呼吸才能说出任何话。所以它非常不稳定。但他确实有声音。

paras.en: Sanders: With time, a live performance with his original voice became impossible. The next option was to use a banked voice, but that wasn’t good enough for a comedy performance.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：随着时间的推移，用他原来的声音进行现场表演变得不可能了。下一个选择是使用银行声音，但这对于喜剧表演来说还不够好。

paras.en: MA: So then he started to lose his voice and he was like, I don’t, you know, I can’t pull this off with a banked voice because it’s so robotic. It’s monotone. You can’t really do it.
paras.zh: MA：然后他开始失去声音，他说，我不知道，你知道，我无法用固定的声音来完成这个任务，因为它太机械了。很单调。你真的做不到。

paras.en: Sanders: Jules couldn’t pull off a comedy show. But could there be a different way, a different voice?
paras.zh: 桑德斯：朱尔斯无法完成喜剧表演。但能否有不同的方式、不同的声音呢？

paras.en: I’m going to step back here and give you more context about Jules and about ALS. ALS is progressive and relentless, which means over time, more and more of the motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord are affected, and symptoms get worse.
paras.zh: 我将回到这里，为您提供有关 Jules 和 ALS 的更多背景信息。 ALS 是进行性且持续的，这意味着随着时间的推移，大脑和脊髓中越来越多的运动神经元受到影响，症状会变得更糟。

paras.en: And though this progression varies quite a bit from person to person, the median survival time after an ALS diagnosis is about 30 months. Time is short here. This diagnosis forces big choices about how to live and what a person wants their remaining time to include, for them and for their family. In the middle of everything else going on, Jules was facing a choice that many people in his situation must confront, whether or not he would get a tracheostomy.
paras.zh: 尽管这种进展因人而异，但 ALS 诊断后的中位生存时间约为 30 个月。这里时间很短。这一诊断迫使人们做出重大选择，决定如何生活，以及一个人希望在剩下的时间里为自己和家人做什么。在所有其他事情发生的过程中，朱尔斯面临着许多与他处境相同的人必须面对的选择，无论他是否接受气管切开术。

paras.en: That’s a procedure in which doctors place a tube in the throat. This tube is then connected to a ventilator that breathes for a person.
paras.zh: 这是医生将一根管子插入喉咙的手术。然后将该管连接到为人呼吸的呼吸机。

paras.en: The procedure can leave a person unable to speak again, with whatever residual voice they might have left. Now, we have spent this episode on what it feels like to lose your voice. Jules was losing his. So it might seem like this part of the decision wouldn’t matter all that much. But to a person who’s losing their voice, and to their family, this moment marks an end point. It’s a hard stop.
paras.zh: 该手术可能会使一个人无法再说话，无论他们可能剩下什么声音。现在，我们用这一集来探讨失去声音的感觉。朱尔斯正在失去他的。因此，这部分决定似乎并不那么重要。但对于一个失声的人和他们的家人来说，这一刻标志着一个终点。这是一个艰难的停止。

paras.en: MA: He was someone who didn’t want to do a tracheostomy. He was opting for, once I’m done, that’s it. And that was our plan.
paras.zh: MA：他是一个不想做气管切开术的人。他选择的是，一旦我完成了，就这样了。这就是我们的计划。

paras.en: Sanders: As Jules and MA confront this decision, could a different sort of voice change the story?
paras.zh: 桑德斯：当朱尔斯和马萨诸塞州面临这个决定时，不同的声音可以改变这个故事吗？

paras.en: Jules: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice.
paras.zh: 朱尔斯：所以当我第一次听到我的克隆声音时，感觉就像我重新出现了一样。当我妻子第一次听到这首歌时，她哭了，因为这听起来太像我失声之前的我了。

paras.en: Sanders: This is The Deep End. Talk to me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot.
paras.zh: 桑德斯：这就是深渊。跟我说话。我是劳拉·桑德斯。如果您喜欢这个播客，请告诉您的朋友并给我们留下评论。对节目帮助很大。

paras.en: Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org. The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. Nancy Schute is our editor in chief. Our music is by Blue Dot Sessions. The podcast is made possible in part by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund with support from PRX.
paras.zh: 请通过 podcasts@sciencenews.org 将您的问题和意见发送给我们。 《The Deep End》是《科学新闻》的制作。它基于我劳拉·桑德斯的原创报道。本集由 Ella Rowen 制作和混音。我们的项目经理是阿什利·耶格尔。南希·舒特 (Nancy Schute) 是我们的主编。我们的音乐是由 Blue Dot Sessions 制作的。该播客的部分制作是由 Burroughs Wellcome 基金在 PRX 的支持下完成的。

paras.en: This podcast was produced with support from the Burroughs Wellcome Fund and in partnership with PRX. The podcast logo was created by Neil Webb.
paras.zh: 该播客是在 Burroughs Wellcome 基金的支持下并与 PRX 合作制作的。播客徽标由尼尔·韦伯创建。

articles.title: A duo goes against the tide to explain an origin of human endurance
articles.author: Elizabeth Pennisi

paras.en: Two researchers may have opened floodgates on the debate over why humans can run marathons, swim the English Channel or dive a hundred meters and back on a single breath and their ape cousins can’t.
paras.zh: 两位研究人员可能开启了关于为什么人类可以跑马拉松、游过英吉利海峡或一口气潜水一百米来回的争论，而他们的猿类表亲却不能。

paras.en: Humans evolved endurance for feats like these not just by running down prey on the African savanna, but also by diving for food in lakes or coastal waters, the duo propose September 17 in PaleoAnthropology. The hypothesis adds complexity to a decades-old theory that puts the drivers for evolution exclusively on land. But it coexists with a history of pushback for any water-related ideas.
paras.zh: 两人在 9 月 17 日的《古人类学》杂志上提出，人类不仅通过在非洲大草原上追捕猎物，还通过在湖泊或沿海水域潜水寻找食物来进化出这样的耐力。这一假说使已有数十年历史的理论变得更加复杂，该理论将进化的驱动力完全集中在陆地上。但它与任何与水有关的想法都受到抵制的历史并存。

paras.en: The work is causing ripples among anthropologists. “I could not work out [at first] if this was groundbreaking or dumb,” says Christian Tryon, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.
paras.zh: 这项工作在人类学家中引起了轩然大波。 “一开始我无法弄清楚这是开创性的还是愚蠢的，”康涅狄格大学斯托斯分校的古人类学家克里斯蒂安·特赖恩 (Christian Tryon) 说。

paras.en: In 1960, researchers came up with what’s been called the aquatic ape or waterside hypothesis, which suggested that our ancestors evolved longer legs and other adaptations from swimming for their suppers in watery habitats. Popularized in media accounts but not adequately vetted in peer-reviewed journals, the idea was shunned by the scientific community as additional fossils pointed away from a life in water. More recently, the dominant theory has been that it was landlocked human ancestors who gradually developed our remarkable endurance. “There’s been this reluctance to really think about anything sort of water-related as important in human evolution,” Tryon says.
paras.zh: 1960 年，研究人员提出了所谓的水生猿或水边假说，该假说表明，我们的祖先通过在水生栖息地游泳以获取晚餐而进化出更长的腿和其他适应能力。这一想法在媒体报道中广为流传，但在同行评审期刊中并未得到充分审查，但由于更多的化石表明不存在水中生命，科学界回避了这一想法。最近，主流理论认为，正是内陆人类祖先逐渐发展出了我们非凡的耐力。特赖恩说：“人们一直不愿意真正考虑与水有关的任何事情在人类进化中的重要性。”

paras.en: Yet evolutionary anthropologist Josephine Joordens, a self-professed “water person” who trained as a marine biologist, had long wondered whether coastal life was vital to the evolutionary process, because it provides easy access to both water and land resources. Joordens combined forces with Erika Schagatay, a physiologist at Mid-Sweden University in Östersund, to formulate what they call the “dive first, run later” hypothesis.
paras.zh: 然而，进化人类学家约瑟芬·乔登斯（Josephine Joordens）自称是“水人”，接受过海洋生物学家培训，她长期以来一直想知道沿海生物是否对进化过程至关重要，因为它可以轻松获取水和土地资源。乔登斯与厄斯特松德中瑞典大学生理学家埃里卡·沙加泰 (Erika Schagatay) 合作，提出了他们所谓的“先潜水，后跑步”的假设。

paras.en: Schagatay — herself a freediver — has spent decades observing and monitoring modern sea foraging people such as the Ama in Japan and the Sama-Bajau in Southeast Asia. Joordens studied fossil evidence and combed the literature about aquatic activities. Our evolution “was likely a very complex and very dynamic process,” says Joordens, of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.
paras.zh: 沙加泰本人是一名自由潜水员，她花了数十年的时间观察和监测现代海上觅食人类，例如日本的海女和东南亚的萨玛巴瑶人。乔登斯研究了化石证据并梳理了有关水生活动的文献。德国莱比锡马克斯普朗克进化人类学研究所的乔登斯说，我们的进化“可能是一个非常复杂和动态的过程”。

paras.en: They propose some Homo species wound up shallow-water diving repeatedly about 2 million to 3 million years ago, much the way the Sama-Bajau do today. These people spend four to six hours per day repeatedly diving several meters deep to catch fish and collect shellfish and other food. They evolved bigger spleens than their non-diving counterparts and, it seems, enhanced respiratory and cardiovascular capacity. They have the ability to “pace” breathing periods and breath-holding to avoid fatigue. In our ancestors, that could have paved the way for the cardiorespiratory stamina needed in modern endurance running, Schagatay says.
paras.zh: 他们提出，一些人种在大约 200 万到 300 万年前就反复进行浅水潜水，就像今天的萨玛巴瑶人那样。这些人每天花四到六个小时反复潜入几米深的地方捕鱼、收集贝类和其他食物。他们进化出比非潜水同伴更大的脾脏，并且呼吸和心血管能力似乎得到增强。他们能够“调整”呼吸周期和屏气以避免疲劳。沙加泰说，对于我们的祖先来说，这可能为现代耐力跑所需的心肺耐力铺平了道路。

paras.en: These Homo divers evolved heavy bones to help stay underwater and downward facing noses to keep water out, the two suggest. They eventually passed those endurance-boosting traits on to other populations with lighter bones and a more terrestrial lifestyle.
paras.zh: 两人表示，这些人种潜水员进化出了沉重的骨骼来帮助留在水下，并进化出向下的鼻子来防水。他们最终将这些增强耐力的特征传递给了其他骨骼更轻、生活方式更陆地的人群。

paras.en: The study “shows there is a lot of evidence” for forage diving as an early evolutionary driver, says Leslea Hlusko, a paleobiologist at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana in Burgos, Spain.
paras.zh: 西班牙布尔戈斯国家人类进化研究中心的古生物学家 Leslea Hlusko 表示，这项研究“有大量证据”表明，觅食潜水是早期进化的驱动力。

paras.en: This idea is not a retread of the aquatic ape theory, says Christopher Ruff, a biological anthropologist at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. “Occasional aquatic foraging is quite a different proposal“ from the discredited theory’s primarily aquatic existence and should be taken seriously, Ruff says.
paras.zh: 约翰·霍普金斯大学医学院的生物人类学家克里斯托弗·拉夫说，这个想法并不是对水生猿理论的翻版。拉夫说，“偶尔的水生觅食是一个完全不同的提议”，与这种不可信的主要水生存在的理论截然不同，应该认真对待。

paras.en: Not everyone thinks the dive first idea holds water.
paras.zh: 并非所有人都认为“潜水第一”的想法站得住脚。

paras.en: Multiple factors work against the idea that diving could have helped humans become better endurance runners, says Daniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University. He argues that endurance diving does not require an enhanced aerobic capacity: It slows the heart rate, whereas running speeds it up. He disputes how and why heavy bones arose; they could have developed in people who used their bodies for heavy work and not because such bones helped divers with buoyancy issues. Nor is the downward pointed nose meaningful given that many diving mammals have forward facing noses. Other reasons, such as keeping the air in nostrils moist, were probably more important in selecting for this feature, he says.
paras.zh: 哈佛大学古人类学家丹尼尔·利伯曼 (Daniel Lieberman) 表示，多种因素不利于潜水可以帮助人类成为更好的耐力跑者的观点。他认为耐力潜水不需要增强有氧能力：它会减慢心率，而跑步会加快心率。他对重骨头如何以及为何产生提出了争议。它们可能是在那些用身体从事繁重工作的人身上形成的，而不是因为这些骨头可以帮助潜水员解决浮力问题。考虑到许多潜水哺乳动物的鼻子都朝前，向下尖的鼻子也没有意义。他说，其他原因，例如保持鼻孔内的空气湿润，可能在选择此功能时更重要。

paras.en: What’s more, many people around the world have long relied on running down game for food, says archaeologist Eugène Morin of Trent University in Peterborough, Canada. “Diving is costly and the [caloric] returns are low,” so early humans would not choose to dive if other foraging opportunities existed, he argues.
paras.zh: 加拿大彼得伯勒特伦特大学的考古学家尤金·莫林表示，更重要的是，世界各地的许多人长期以来一直依靠捕猎野味来获取食物。他认为，“潜水成本高昂，而且[热量]回报很低”，因此如果存在其他觅食机会，早期人类不会选择潜水。

paras.en: Critiques aside, “the simple ‘ape walked out from forest to savanna’ story clearly does not cut it anymore,” says Pascal Gagneux, a biological anthropologist at the University of California, San Diego. Coastal routes around Africa, along Africa’s lakeshores and out of Africa “must have played a huge role” in human evolution, Gagneux says.
paras.zh: 抛开批评不谈，“简单的‘猿从森林走到稀树草原’的故事显然已经不再适用了，”加州大学圣地亚哥分校的生物人类学家帕斯卡·加格纽克斯(Pascal Gagneux)说。加格纽克斯说，围绕非洲、沿着非洲湖岸以及走出非洲的沿海路线在人类进化中“一定发挥了巨大作用”。

paras.en: The pair knows they risk the ire of their peers in presenting this “dive first” hypothesis, but Joordens says, “we are both in our early 60s and we both have beautiful careers, so we thought ‘whatever happens, happens.’”
paras.zh: 两人知道提出这种“潜水优先”的假设可能会激怒同侪，但乔登斯说，“我们都 60 岁出头，而且都拥有美好的职业生涯，所以我们认为‘无论发生什么，都会发生。’”

paras.en: And Tryon ultimately found the paper worth the read. “If nothing else, it gets people thinking and it gets people looking.”
paras.zh: 特赖恩最终发现这篇论文值得一读。 “如果不出意外的话，它会让人们思考，让人们寻找。”

articles.title: To turn invisible, we need to tweak the path light travels
articles.author: Sofia Caetano Avritzer

paras.en: It’s pretty hard to fight an opponent you can’t see. That’s what makes Invisible Woman an invaluable member of the Fantastic Four. She can disappear in the blink of an eye and take out entire factions of enemies, all while her adversaries kick and punch empty air.
paras.zh: 与看不见的对手战斗是非常困难的。这就是隐形女侠成为神奇四侠中无价的成员的原因。她可以在眨眼之间消失并消灭整个敌人派系，而她的对手却在空中拳打脚踢。

paras.en: Characters with invisibility powers — Marvel Comics’ Invisible Woman (aka Sue Storm), H.G. Wells’ Invisible Man and The Incredibles’ Violet Parr — can do all sorts of cool things. Escape embarrassing situations. Snoop on other people. Go places where they’re not allowed.
paras.zh: 拥有隐形能力的角色——漫威漫画的隐形女侠（又名苏·斯托姆）、H.G.威尔斯的隐形人和超人总动员的维奥莱特·帕尔——可以做各种很酷的事情。逃离尴尬的境地。窥探其他人。去他们不允许去的地方。

paras.en: Short of a theoretical invisibility cloak, that kind of lurking is impossible for us. But some animals can hide in plain sight by turning nearly transparent.
paras.zh: 如果没有理论上的隐形斗篷，这种潜伏对我们来说是不可能的。但有些动物可以通过变得近乎透明来隐藏在众目睽睽之下。

paras.en: Invisibility is useful for animals that spend a lot of time in places with no good hiding spots, such as the air or open ocean, says Kate Feller, a visual ecologist at Union College in Schenectady, N.Y.
paras.zh: 纽约州斯克内克塔迪联合学院的视觉生态学家凯特·费勒表示，对于那些长时间待在空气或公海等没有良好藏身之处的动物来说，隐形非常有用。

paras.en: The secret to invisibility is all about light. “The way we see things is when light is reflected back off of an object onto our eyes,” Feller says. The more light that can pass through something undisturbed, the harder it is to see that thing.
paras.zh: 隐形的秘密就在于光。 “我们看到事物的方式是光线从物体反射回我们的眼睛，”费勒说。能穿过不受干扰的物体的光线越多，看到该物体就越困难。

paras.en: Light can’t easily pass through most animals, but those with nearly invisible body parts have tricks to get around this hurdle.
paras.zh: 光无法轻易穿过大多数动物，但那些身体部位几乎看不见的动物却有办法绕过这个障碍。

paras.en: Animals get their colors from pigments, compounds that appear as different colors depending on which wavelengths of light they absorb and which they reflect. Green pigments, for instance, reflect green light and absorb all other colors. Invisibility requires getting rid of these colorful compounds.
paras.zh: 动物从颜料和化合物中获得颜色，这些化合物根据它们吸收和反射的光波长而呈现不同的颜色。例如，绿色颜料反射绿光并吸收所有其他颜色。隐形需要摆脱这些彩色化合物。

paras.en: Most baby fish lack pigments at first, helping them hide from predators. Some species stay see-through their whole lives. One is the ghost catfish (Kryptopterus vitreolus). With a body that’s fully transparent from gills to tail, it looks like a floating head from afar.
paras.zh: 大多数幼鱼一开始都缺乏色素，这有助于它们躲避捕食者。有些物种一生都保持透明。其中一种是幽灵鲶鱼（Kryptopterus vitreolus）。它的身体从鳃到尾巴都是完全透明的，远远望去就像一个漂浮的头。

paras.en: It’s hard to hide every body part, though. Eyes need light-absorbing pigments to see. And even clear stomachs will show up if animals eat colorful food. A ghost catfish eats only small bits of food and its long, thin, tubelike stomach stretches out a meal, helping the organ stay hidden, says Qibin Zhao, a physicist and materials scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China. Blood can’t be transparent either due to the iron-rich hemoglobin molecules that carry oxygen. So up close, the ghost catfish’s blood vessels are still visible.
paras.zh: 不过，很难隐藏身体的每一个部位。眼睛需要吸收光的色素才能看到东西。如果动物吃彩色食物，甚至会出现清澈的胃。中国上海交通大学的物理学家兼材料科学家赵其斌说，幽灵鲶鱼只吃少量食物，它又长又薄的管状胃可以伸出食物，帮助该器官隐藏起来。由于富含铁的血红蛋白分子携带氧气，血液也不透明。所以近距离观察，鬼鲶鱼的血管依然清晰可见。

paras.en: But even pigment-free objects are not entirely invisible. Light travels at different speeds through different materials so will bend or bounce when it goes from one material to another. That can create a shine, like sun reflecting off a puddle.
paras.zh: 但即使是无色素的物体也不是完全看不见的。光以不同的速度穿过不同的材料，因此当它从一种材料传播到另一种材料时会弯曲或反弹。这可以产生光泽，就像阳光从水坑反射一样。

paras.en: That’s not a big problem for a glasswing butterfly (Greta oto): Its wings have fewer reflective scales than other butterflies’ wings. The wings are also covered in tiny wax bumps that make light’s transition from air to tissue more gradual, so light passes through the wings mostly undisturbed.
paras.zh: 对于玻璃翅蝴蝶（Greta oto）来说，这不是一个大问题：它的翅膀比其他蝴蝶的翅膀具有更少的反光鳞片。翅膀上还覆盖着微小的蜡块，使光线从空气到组织的过渡更加平缓，因此光线穿过翅膀时基本上不受干扰。

paras.en: Invisible Woman uses a completely different vanishing trick than real-life transparent animals. Instead of letting light pass through her, she bends lights rays to completely avoid her body. The rays never even touch her, so they are not reflected or absorbed, making her invisible to any onlookers.
paras.zh: 隐形女侠使用了与现实生活中的透明动物完全不同的消失技巧。她没有让光线穿过她，而是弯曲光线以完全避开她的身体。光线甚至从未接触过她，因此不会被反射或吸收，使任何旁观者都看不到她。

paras.en: In 2006, scientists proposed that this same logic could be used to create an invisibility cloak. But in practice, a material that perfectly bends light rays is expensive, hard to make and can divert only a narrow band of light at a time. That’s just enough to make a single-colored object disappear but not an entire human.
paras.zh: 2006年，科学家提出同样的逻辑可以用来制造隐形斗篷。但在实践中，能够完美弯曲光线的材料价格昂贵，难以制造，并且一次只能转移很窄的光带。这足以使一个单色物体消失，但不足以使整个人消失。

paras.en: And there’s another problem: With no light getting into the cloak, a person inside can’t see out. Luckily, Sue Storm has the ability to use cosmic rays to see while she’s invisible, allowing her to protect the world from supervillains like Doctor Doom.
paras.zh: 还有另一个问题：斗篷里没有光线，里面的人看不到外面。幸运的是，苏·斯托姆有能力利用宇宙射线在隐形状态下看到东西，这让她能够保护世界免受末日博士等超级恶棍的侵害。

articles.title: Scientists Had Mice Eat Olive Oil Before Carbs, And It Changed Their Blood Sugar Response
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: One of the core challenges in diabetes is controlling your blood sugar after eating, particularly when carbohydrates are involved.
paras.zh: 糖尿病的核心挑战之一是控制饭后血糖，尤其是涉及碳水化合物时。

paras.en: But new findings give further evidence that it's not just what you eat that matters when it comes to controlling blood glucose – when you eat is also an important factor.
paras.zh: 但新的发现进一步证明，在控制血糖方面，重要的不仅仅是吃什么，什么时候吃也是一个重要因素。

paras.en: In a study published in Diabetes, researchers found that mice fed olive oil before consuming glucose saw a reduced increase in blood sugar afterward.
paras.zh: 在《糖尿病》杂志上发表的一项研究中，研究人员发现，在摄入葡萄糖之前喂食橄榄油的小鼠随后的血糖升高有所减少。

paras.en: "Our findings suggest that the order in which nutrients reach the gut can engage a coordinated hormone-nerve response that changes how quickly the stomach delivers glucose to the intestine," says endocrinologist Daisuke Yabe from Kyoto University.
paras.zh: 京都大学内分泌学家矢部大辅 (Daisuke Yabe) 表示：“我们的研究结果表明，营养物质到达肠道的顺序可以引起激素神经反应的协调，从而改变胃将葡萄糖输送到肠道的速度。”

paras.en: While the new findings have only been demonstrated in mice for now, it's not the first time we've seen evidence that the order foods are eaten can affect how blood sugar levels respond after a meal.
paras.zh: 虽然新发现目前仅在小鼠身上得到证实，但这并不是我们第一次看到证据表明进食顺序会影响餐后血糖水平的反应。

paras.en: Meal-sequencing is an emerging dietary approach to help treat and manage diabetes and obesity, with evidence showing that eating vegetables or foods rich in protein or in fat prior to eating carbohydrates helps to keep people's blood sugar lower.
paras.zh: 膳食顺序是一种新兴的饮食方法，有助于治疗和控制糖尿病和肥胖症，有证据表明，在吃碳水化合物之前先吃蔬菜或富含蛋白质或脂肪的食物有助于降低人们的血糖。

paras.en: It's thought that this could be due to certain nutrients slowing the process of gastric emptying, which means food moves more slowly into the small intestine, delaying the absorption of glucose into the bloodstream.
paras.zh: 人们认为，这可能是由于某些营养物质减缓了胃排空过程，这意味着食物更缓慢地进入小肠，从而延迟了葡萄糖吸收到血液中。

paras.en: Another possibility is that eating some foods before carbs may induce the secretion of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) – the appetite-suppressing and insulin-boosting hormone mimicked by drugs like Ozempic.
paras.zh: 另一种可能性是，在吃碳水化合物之前吃一些食物可能会诱导胰高血糖素样肽-1 (GLP-1) 的分泌，这是一种抑制食欲和促进胰岛素的激素，类似于 Ozempic 等药物。

paras.en: To explore these mechanisms further, Yabe's team conducted an experiment with mice, evaluating three separate conditions after an overnight fast.
paras.zh: 为了进一步探索这些机制，Yabe 的团队对小鼠进行了一项实验，评估了禁食过夜后的三种不同条件。

paras.en: In one test, mice were given olive oil 15 minutes before being given glucose. Another group received glucose first, then olive oil. A third group of mice served as controls, consuming water followed by glucose.
paras.zh: 在一项测试中，小鼠在服用葡萄糖前 15 分钟服用橄榄油。另一组首先接受葡萄糖，然后接受橄榄油。第三组小鼠作为对照组，先喝水，然后喝葡萄糖。

paras.en: Blood tests after the feeding experiment showed that mice fed olive oil before the glucose had significantly lower blood glucose immediately after the meal, with marked reductions at the 15- and 30-minute marks compared to the other mice, although the effects appeared to diminish by 60 minutes.
paras.zh: 喂养实验后的血液测试表明，在喂食葡萄糖之前喂橄榄油的小鼠在餐后立即显着降低了血糖，与其他小鼠相比，在 15 分钟和 30 分钟时血糖明显降低，尽管这种影响似乎在 60 分钟后减弱。

paras.en: The mice fed olive oil first also showed slower gastric emptying and had higher levels of the hormones glucagon, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), and GLP-1 in their blood – suggesting a range of hormonal responses that may help slow gastric emptying and limit blood sugar spikes.
paras.zh: 首先喂食橄榄油的小鼠还表现出胃排空较慢，并且血液中胰高血糖素、葡萄糖依赖性促胰岛素多肽 (GIP) 和 GLP-1 激素水平较高，这表明一系列激素反应可能有助于减缓胃排空并限制血糖峰值。

paras.en: The researchers tested other fats in addition to olive oil, including flaxseed oil, lard, coconut oil, and fish oil. Olive oil generally performed the best in terms of controlling blood sugar, although flaxseed oil and lard produced similar results in some measures.
paras.zh: 研究人员测试了除橄榄油外的其他脂肪，包括亚麻籽油、猪油、椰子油和鱼油。尽管亚麻籽油和猪油在某些方面产生了相似的结果，但橄榄油在控制血糖方面通常表现最好。

paras.en: In separate experiments using mouse models of diabetes, pre-loaded olive oil offered similar benefits to blood sugar and gastric emptying, suggesting the mechanism operates even when the body's ability to produce insulin is substantially reduced.
paras.zh: 在使用糖尿病小鼠模型的单独实验中，预装橄榄油对血糖和胃排空也有类似的好处，这表明即使身体产生胰岛素的能力大幅降低，该机制也会发挥作用。

paras.en: In other tests using drugs and genetically engineered mice, the researchers blocked the animals' glucagon and GLP-1 signaling. They found that if one of these pathways was disrupted, olive oil still had beneficial effects, but if both pathways were blocked, the blood sugar reduction was weakened or lost, and the effects to slow gastric emptying vanished.
paras.zh: 在使用药物和基因工程小鼠的其他测试中，研究人员阻断了动物的胰高血糖素和 GLP-1 信号传导。他们发现，如果其中一条途径被破坏，橄榄油仍然具有有益作用，但如果两条途径都被阻断，血糖降低作用就会减弱或消失，并且减缓胃排空的作用就会消失。

paras.en: Similarly, in a final experiment, the researchers found that if they surgically disrupted vagus nerve signaling in mice, olive oil's ability to mitigate blood sugar increases and slow gastric emptying was weakened or no longer detectable, even though the animals' hormonal responses remained intact.
paras.zh: 同样，在最后的实验中，研究人员发现，如果他们通过手术破坏小鼠的迷走神经信号，橄榄油缓解血糖升高和减缓胃排空的能力就会减弱或不再可检测到，即使动物的激素反应保持不变。

paras.en: Taken together, it looks like olive oil's benefits to control blood sugar involve both hormones and neural pathways, the team thinks.
paras.zh: 研究小组认为，总的来说，橄榄油控制血糖的好处似乎涉及激素和神经通路。

paras.en: "The effect appears to involve an integrated endocrine-neural response rather than a single hormone," the researchers write.
paras.zh: 研究人员写道：“这种效应似乎涉及综合的内分泌神经反应，而不是单一的激素。”

paras.en: "These observations suggest that early nutrient sensing activates coordinated endocrine responses that contribute to slowing gastric emptying and limiting glucose excursions."
paras.zh: “这些观察结果表明，早期营养感应激活协调的内分泌反应，有助于减缓胃排空和限制葡萄糖波动。”

paras.en: Given that olive oil doesn't show the same benefits if it's consumed after glucose, the order of the nutrients is a controlling factor, the study authors say.
paras.zh: 研究作者说，考虑到在葡萄糖之后食用橄榄油不会表现出同样的好处，因此营养素的顺序是一个控制因素。

paras.en: It's possible that if glucose is eaten first, its rapid absorption into the bloodstream may suppress the responsiveness of pancreatic alpha cells, impairing their ability to release glucagon in response to fatty acids. By contrast, consuming olive oil first may activate fatty acid-sensing mechanisms before blood glucose levels rise substantially.
paras.zh: 如果先吃葡萄糖，它可能会被快速吸收到血液中，从而抑制胰腺α细胞的反应，从而削弱它们响应脂肪酸而释放胰高血糖素的能力。相比之下，首先食用橄榄油可能会在血糖水平大幅上升之前激活脂肪酸感应机制。

paras.en: There's still a lot we don't fully know about this mechanism, and it's worth reiterating that these olive oil effects have so far only been shown in mice, with no guarantee we'd see the same benefits in human patients.
paras.zh: 关于这种机制，我们还有很多不完全了解的地方，值得重申的是，迄今为止，这些橄榄油的作用仅在小鼠身上得到了证实，不能保证我们会在人类患者身上看到同样的好处。

paras.en: But the findings highlight a common ingredient that researchers might easily be able to test in people in future studies, and give us some new clues toward a better understanding of the ways meal sequencing may work.
paras.zh: 但这些发现强调了一种常见成分，研究人员可以在未来的研究中轻松地在人体中测试这种成分，并为我们提供一些新线索，帮助我们更好地理解膳食测序的工作原理。

paras.en: "Our group has long been interested in practical dietary approaches that people can continue in everyday life," Yabe says.
paras.zh: “我们的团队长期以来一直对人们可以在日常生活中继续使用的实用饮食方法感兴趣，”亚部说。

paras.en: "Meal-sequencing is appealing because it merely changes how a meal is eaten rather than requiring people to avoid entire food groups."
paras.zh: “进餐顺序很有吸引力，因为它仅仅改变了进餐的方式，而不是要求人们避开整个食物组。”

articles.title: FDA-Approved Drug Could Be Repurposed to Relieve Osteoarthritis Pain And Protect Cartilage
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: Researchers are always looking out for drugs that can be repurposed for something else. The main benefit is that these treatments have already passed various safety tests, which means they can be made available more quickly for new conditions.
paras.zh: 研究人员一直在寻找可以重新用于其他用途的药物。主要好处是这些治疗方法已经通过了各种安全测试，这意味着它们可以更快地用于新情况。

paras.en: Now a team from the Yale School of Medicine in the US has discovered that the epilepsy drug lacosamide could also be effective in cases of osteoarthritis – not just easing the associated pain, but also reversing some of the damage it causes to joints.
paras.zh: 现在，美国耶鲁大学医学院的一个研究小组发现，癫痫药物拉科酰胺对骨关节炎也有效，不仅可以缓解相关疼痛，还可以逆转其对关节造成的部分损伤。

paras.en: Osteoarthritis is when the cushioning, lubricating cartilage between bones gets damaged and worn away. Current treatments can manage the pain, but there's no real fix besides replacement surgery (which can come with its own issues).
paras.zh: 骨关节炎是指骨头之间的缓冲、润滑软骨受损和磨损。目前的治疗方法可以控制疼痛，但除了替代手术（这可能会带来其自身的问题）之外，没有真正的解决办法。

paras.en: The results of the lacosamide tests, published in Bioactive Materials, show that in mouse models and human cartilage cells in the lab, it's capable of encouraging cartilage repair, slowing its deterioration, and reducing the pain that goes with it.
paras.zh: 发表在《生物活性材料》上的拉科酰胺测试结果表明，在实验室的小鼠模型和人类软骨细胞中，它能够促进软骨修复，减缓其恶化，并减轻随之而来的疼痛。

paras.en: In addition, the researchers identified a 'sweet spot' where the drug was most beneficial, which will be useful in developing the treatment further.
paras.zh: 此外，研究人员还确定了药物最有益的“最佳点”，这将有助于进一步开发治疗方法。

paras.en: "There is an optimal range where the drug helps restore balance without overcorrecting," says musculoskeletal biologist Chuan-Ju Liu. "What stood out was not just its effectiveness, but how little of a dose was needed."
paras.zh: 肌肉骨骼生物学家 Chuan-Ju Liu 说：“药物有一个最佳范围，可以帮助恢复平衡而不过度矫正。” “最突出的不仅仅是它的有效性，而是只需要很少的剂量。”

paras.en: "This tells us the system is finely tuned."
paras.zh: “这告诉我们这个系统经过了精心调整。”

paras.en: The researchers were led to lacosamide because it's a sodium channel blocker. In a previous study, some of the same researchers identified a sodium channel and protein called Nav1.7 as being involved in both sending pain signals to the brain and regulating how cartilage is built up and broken down.
paras.zh: 研究人员选择了拉科酰胺，因为它是一种钠通道阻滞剂。在之前的一项研究中，一些研究人员发现了一种名为 Nav1.7 的钠通道和蛋白质参与向大脑发送疼痛信号以及调节软骨的形成和分解。

paras.en: Nav1.7 is active inside special cells called chondrocytes, which manage the balance of removing old tissue and adding new tissue. Osteoarthritis disrupts this balance, tipping the scales towards cartilage loss, and Nav1.7 is an important factor in that. In a joint affected by osteoarthritis, Nav1.7 is more active than it should be.
paras.zh: Nav1.7 在称为软骨细胞的特殊细胞内活跃，软骨细胞管理去除旧组织和添加新组织的平衡。骨关节炎破坏了这种平衡，导致软骨损失，而 Nav1.7 是其中的一个重要因素。在受骨关节炎影响的关节中，Nav1.7 比应有的状态更加活跃。

paras.en: "When Nav1.7 becomes dysregulated, it contributes to both joint degeneration and pain," says Liu.
paras.zh: “当 Nav1.7 失调时，就会导致关节退化和疼痛，”Liu 说。

paras.en: "Our findings suggest that Nav1.7 is a dual-acting target. By blocking this single protein, we can potentially quiet the pain nerves and tell the cartilage cells to not only stop breaking down but start repairing as well."
paras.zh: “我们的研究结果表明 Nav1.7 是一个双重作用靶点。通过阻断这种单一蛋白质，我们可以潜在地平息疼痛神经，并告诉软骨细胞不仅停止分解，而且开始修复。”

paras.en: Essentially, lacosamide is dialing down the activity of Nav1.7, and the published research shows the impact it can have on cartilage and pain.
paras.zh: 从本质上讲，拉科酰胺正在降低 Nav1.7 的活性，已发表的研究显示了它对软骨和疼痛的影响。

paras.en: The team also wanted to find the best way to administer the drug, and found that injecting it directly into the affected joint in mice worked better than giving it orally, even at lower doses.
paras.zh: 研究小组还希望找到最好的给药方式，并发现将其直接注射到小鼠受影响的关节中比口服给药效果更好，即使剂量较低。

paras.en: The catch was that it didn't stick around for long once it was in there, meaning repeat injections were needed to keep it working.
paras.zh: 问题是，它一旦进入体内就不会停留太久，这意味着需要重复注射才能保持其发挥作用。

paras.en: In the injection tests, lacosamide was packed inside a gel to counteract the 'leaky bucket' nature of joints that can quickly dissipate any liquid treatments.
paras.zh: 在注射测试中，拉科酰胺被包装在凝胶内，以抵消关节的“漏桶”性质，这种性质可以快速消散任何液体治疗。

paras.en: "The hydrogel acts as a local reservoir," says Liu. "It holds the drug in place in the location it is needed most and releases it slowly over time. It transforms a daily pill into a long-lasting, local treatment that stays active for a month or longer."
paras.zh: “水凝胶充当当地的水库，”刘说。 “它将药物固定在最需要的位置，并随着时间的推移缓慢释放。它将每日服用的药物转变为持久的局部治疗方法，可以保持一个月或更长时间的活性。”

paras.en: All of this needs to be tested on actual osteoarthritis patients, of course, but the early signs are promising. As we mentioned at the start, the status of lacosamide as an approved epilepsy drug means the time to clinical tests should be shorter.
paras.zh: 当然，所有这些都需要在实际的骨关节炎患者身上进行测试，但早期迹象是有希望的。正如我们在开始时提到的，拉科酰胺作为已批准的癫痫药物的地位意味着临床测试的时间应该更短。

paras.en: Past research suggests lacosamide can indeed be effective as a painkiller, though the previous work was related to a different Nav1.7-related condition.
paras.zh: 过去的研究表明拉科酰胺确实可以作为止痛药有效，尽管之前的研究与不同的 Nav1.7 相关病症有关。

paras.en: If the drug can be developed further for osteoarthritis, then the potential is huge for the hundreds of millions of people with osteoarthritis worldwide: a drug that doesn't just numb the pain of the condition, but also brings back lost cartilage.
paras.zh: 如果这种药物能够进一步开发用于治疗骨关节炎，那么对于全世界数亿骨关节炎患者来说，潜力是巨大的：这种药物不仅可以麻痹病情的疼痛，还可以恢复失去的软骨。

paras.en: "There is a major unmet need in osteoarthritis," says Liu. "We need therapies that don't just mask pain but actually change how the disease progresses."
paras.zh: “骨关节炎方面存在重大未满足的需求，”刘说。 “我们需要的疗法不仅能掩盖疼痛，还能真正改变疾病的进展方式。”

paras.en: The research has been published in Bioactive Materials.
paras.zh: 该研究已发表在《生物活性材料》上。

articles.title: Microbe Discovered With One of The Smallest Genomes on Record, Pushing The Bounds of What It Means to Be Alive
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: A tiny microbe detected inside a marine plankton has one of the smallest genomes of any organism ever found, and it's really putting biologists' definition of 'life' to the test.
paras.zh: 在海洋浮游生物中检测到的一种微小微生物具有迄今为止发现的任何生物体中最小的基因组之一，这确实使生物学家对“生命”的定义受到了考验。

paras.en: The team of researchers who first came across this mote of life weren't even looking for it.
paras.zh: 第一次发现这种生命微粒的研究团队甚至没有去寻找它。

paras.en: They were collecting single-celled plankton, Citharistes regius, swimming in surface seawater off the coast of Shimoda in Japan.
paras.zh: 他们正在日本下田海岸附近的表层海水中采集单细胞浮游生物 Citharistes regius。

paras.en: Citharistes regius survives with the help of photosynthesizing cyanobacteria, and the researchers profiled the genetic material of these bacteria to better understand how this symbiosis evolved.
paras.zh: Citharistes regius 在进行光合作用的蓝细菌的帮助下生存，研究人员分析了这些细菌的遗传物质，以更好地了解这种共生关系是如何进化的。

paras.en: But among the genomes they discovered, there was a strange, tiny loop of genetic material, made up of just 238 kilobase pairs (kbps) of DNA: barely enough to sustain life, as far as we know.
paras.zh: 但在他们发现的基因组中，有一个奇怪的微小遗传物质环，仅由 238 千碱基对 (kbps) 的 DNA 组成：据我们所知，这几乎不足以维持生命。

paras.en: In a new paper published in Current Biology, an international team of biologists and computer scientists have come together to describe this baffling entity.
paras.zh: 在《当代生物学》上发表的一篇新论文中，一个由生物学家和计算机科学家组成的国际团队聚集在一起描述了这个令人困惑的实体。

paras.en: They've named it Sukunaarchaeum mirabile, after a Shinto spirit named Sukuna known for his small size and power.
paras.zh: 他们将其命名为 Sukunaarchaeum mirabile，以神道教神灵 Sukuna 的名字命名，该神灵因其体型小而力量大而闻名。

paras.en: It's a member of the domain Archaea. Archaea were long mistaken for bacteria because, like bacteria, they're single-celled and their DNA is not packaged up inside a membrane-bound nucleus.
paras.zh: 它是古菌域的成员。古细菌长期以来一直被误认为是细菌，因为和细菌一样，它们是单细胞的，并且它们的 DNA 没有包装在膜结合的细胞核内。

paras.en: But archaea have a distinct evolutionary history from bacteria, and many unique traits to show for it.
paras.zh: 但古细菌具有与细菌不同的进化历史，并显示出许多独特的特征。

paras.en: Archaea are always pretty small, but Sukunaarchaeum mirabile sets a new record. Scientists have never before seen an archaeon with a genome this tiny.
paras.zh: 古细菌总是很小，但 Sukunaarchaeum mirabile 创造了新的记录。科学家们此前从未见过基因组如此之小的古细菌。

paras.en: There are viruses with genomes larger than this microbe, with some reaching 730,000 base pairs or even 2.5 million. And by mainstream definitions, those don't even qualify as living things, since viruses don't have their own metabolisms.
paras.zh: 有些病毒的基因组比这种微生物还要大，有的达到 73 万个碱基对，甚至 250 万个碱基对。根据主流定义，它们甚至不符合生物的资格，因为病毒没有自己的新陈代谢。

paras.en: Sukunaarchaeum is missing almost all the genes it would need to maintain its metabolism, which is why, when the preprint was released back in 2025, we reported that the microbe led a 'virus-like' existence.
paras.zh: Sukunaarchaeum 几乎缺失了维持其新陈代谢所需的所有基因，这就是为什么当 2025 年预印本发布时，我们报告说这种微生物过着“类似病毒”的存在。

paras.en: "The near-complete absence of recognizable metabolic pathways in Sukunaarchaeum suggests that it can neither sustain itself independently nor provide an obvious metabolic benefit to its host," the researchers explain.
paras.zh: 研究人员解释说：“Sukunaarchaeum 中几乎完全缺乏可识别的代谢途径，这表明它既不能独立维持自身，也不能为其宿主提供明显的代谢益处。”

paras.en: But the final, published version of the paper drops that analogy, presumably to avoid confusion about the microbe's true taxonomic classification.
paras.zh: 但该论文的最终发布版本放弃了这种类比，大概是为了避免对微生物的真正分类学分类产生混淆。

paras.en: "The key to defining life is whether something can replicate itself, and whether it can do this autonomously," explains molecular biologist Thorsten Allers, of the University of Nottingham.
paras.zh: 诺丁汉大学的分子生物学家托尔斯滕·阿勒斯解释说：“定义生命的关键是某些东西是否可以自我复制，以及它是否可以自主地复制自己。”

paras.en: "This exciting discovery provides new clues about how simple a living cell can become while remaining capable of reproducing and maintaining its own genetic information."
paras.zh: “这一令人兴奋的发现提供了新的线索，说明活细胞可以变得多么简单，同时仍然能够复制和维持其自身的遗传信息。”

paras.en: The only other organisms with fewer pieces of DNA than Sukunaarchaeum are bacteria that have become so dependent on a symbiotic host, they've almost lost their identity as a separate organism.
paras.zh: 唯一比 Sukunaarchaeum 拥有更少 DNA 片段的生物是细菌，它们已经变得如此依赖于共生宿主，以至于它们几乎失去了作为独立生物体的身份。

paras.en: This is how more complex cells, including our own, may have come about.
paras.zh: 这就是更复杂的细胞（包括我们自己的细胞）可能产生的方式。

paras.en: For instance, it's how scientists explain the fact that our mitochondria have their own separate set of conserved DNA: free-living bacteria, they say, moved inside eukaryotic cells, and 1.5 billion years later, they're still in there, now an integral part of us.
paras.zh: 例如，科学家们就是这样解释我们的线粒体有自己独立的一组保守DNA的：他们说，自由生活的细菌在真核细胞内移动，15亿年后，它们仍然在那里，现在是我们不可分割的一部分。

paras.en: Perhaps Sukunaarchaeum mirabile, which scientists know only via its genome and have yet to see through a microscope, is also in the process of merging with its host.
paras.zh: 也许Sukunaarchaeum mirabile（科学家们只能通过其基因组来了解它，尚未通过显微镜观察）也正在与其宿主融合。

paras.en: But for the mutual benefit of the relationship, endosymbionts need a metabolism to give something back to their host. That's why the researchers are instead proposing that Sukunaarchaeum may be a parasite.
paras.zh: 但为了这种关系的共同利益，内共生体需要新陈代谢来回馈宿主。这就是为什么研究人员提出 Sukunaarchaeum 可能是一种寄生虫。

paras.en: If that's the case, it would be only the second parasitic archaeon on record.
paras.zh: 如果真是这样，这将是有记录以来的第二个寄生古菌。

paras.en: Another clue that its lifestyle may be parasitic is that a quarter of its genome is dedicated to producing large membrane proteins. These same proteins have been seen in the only other known parasitic archaea, weaponized as a way to invade a host.
paras.zh: 其生活方式可能是寄生的另一个线索是其基因组的四分之一专门用于产生大型膜蛋白。这些相同的蛋白质在唯一已知的寄生古菌中也被发现，被武器化作为入侵宿主的一种方式。

paras.en: "Although [Sukunaarchaeum] has lost almost all of the genes needed to make nutrients and energy, it has kept much of the machinery required to copy its genome and produce proteins from its genetic information," says Allers.
paras.zh: “尽管[Sukunaarchaeum]已经失去了几乎所有制造营养和能量所需的基因，但它保留了复制其基因组并从其遗传信息中生产蛋白质所需的大部分机制，”阿勒斯说。

paras.en: "This suggests that Sukunaarchaeum may be close to the minimum level of genetic information needed for an organism to remain an independent cell."
paras.zh: “这表明 Sukunaarchaeum 可能接近有机体保持独立细胞所需的最低遗传信息水平。”

paras.en: The research has been published in Current Biology.
paras.zh: 该研究已发表在《当代生物学》上。

articles.title: This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain

paras.en: This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
paras.zh: 这种微小的侏罗纪掠食者为人类大脑铺平了道路

paras.en: A tiny, 165-million-year-old Jurassic predator reveals an evolutionary breakthrough that helped pave the way for modern mammals and the human brain.
paras.zh: 一只 1.65 亿年前的侏罗纪小型捕食者揭示了一项进化突破，为现代哺乳动物和人类大脑铺平了道路。

paras.en: - A 165-million-year-old fossil has revealed an extraordinary Jurassic predator that may help explain how mammals developed one of their most important evolutionary advantages. Although only 20 inches long, Megacauda sungei was a heavyweight among early mammal relatives, swimming through ancient waterways and hunting prey with specialized teeth.
