It adds that damage to cameras, sensors, or blind-spot monitoring systems may not be visible from the exterior, but can “significantly affect repair needs and safety.”

“Allstate’s Auto Lab includes electric and hybrid vehicles specifically to train claims adjusters on these considerations, using the same diagnostic tools many repair facilities use,” the release states.

articles.title: Understanding Honda’s Variable Valve Timing System
articles.author: Jerry Renshaw

paras.en: It’s been understood for a long time that being able to control valve lift, duration and timing is a great way to optimize various aspects of engine performance. It can enhance power, throttle response, fuel economy and emissions, and engine designers have devised hydraulic, electro-hydraulic and even “camless” systems that use poppet valves rather than a conventional valve train. With stricter emissions standards in place, many manufacturers see variable valve timing (VVT) as a good way to hit those targets.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A lumpy racing cam can introduce a lot more air into the combustion chambers, enhancing efficiency, but that usually means a rough idle and possible drivability problems at lower RPMs. A less aggressive cam might mean a smooth idle, but when intake valves close too early at higher engine speeds it can compromise performance. If both intake and exhaust valves are open, even just momentarily, it can cause unburnt fuel to exit the engine or can push unburnt gases back into the intake manifold.

Earlier VVT systems were two-step designs, with one timing profile for engine speeds below 3500 RPM or so, and another timing and lift profile for engine speeds above 3500 RPM. Newer VVTs are designed for infinite adjustment throughout the RPM range.

VVT systems date back as far as early aircraft engines and even steam locomotives, while Fiat was the first manufacturer to introduce a successful VVT design in the late ‘60s. One of the most successful and reliable systems, though, has been Honda’s Variable Valve Timing and Lift Electronic Control (VTEC) and i-VTEC designs. Honda’s systems have been around since model year 1989. Let’s take a closer look.

Any VVT system is designed to change the relationship between the crankshaft and camshaft. Older, simpler systems use a phaser that enables a range of adjustment, but only for valve timing and not lift and duration. Here’s a quick breakdown of how VTEC performs:
As RPMs go up, the engine management computer directs oil through the rocker shaft (the horizontal tube that runs through all the rocker arms).
As this oil pressure goes up, a pin is actuated and slides through the low-RPM rocker arms, locking them together with a third high-RPM rocker arm.

Each cylinder has a third lobe on the camshaft, situated between the lobes for intake and exhaust valves, and this third rocker arm follows that lobe and its profile to optimize valvetrain operation for higher engine speeds.

This technology was first explored on Honda’s motorcycle engine, then Honda’s New Engine Concept project (unveiled in 1984) helped convince the OEM’s management that a dynamic cam phasing system was a good feature for enhancing engine performance.

The i-VTEC (“i” for Intelligent) debuted in 2001 and uses an adjustable cam gear that’s actuated by oil pressure. The ECM constantly monitors engine load and RPMs to make adjustments to cam timing in real time, while the VTEC system only kicks in at about 4000 RPMs or more. i-VTEC is available in two different iterations: one for performance engines (think Civic Si or Acura TSX) and one for economy and daily drivers (think Accord or CR-V). With i-VTEC setups, the camshaft for intake valves can be adjustable from 25 to 50 degrees, from fully retarded at idle to mild advance at full throttle.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: i-VTEC is still featured in select naturally-aspirated models, including the Civic, HR-V and CR-V, although it’s gradually being phased out in favor of turbocharging and more standard VTC systems. It can still be found in Honda’s K-series, R-series, J-series and L-series engine families.

In economy setups, with four valves per cylinder, VTEC-E can effectively make the engine operate as a 12-valve by shutting down one intake valve at lower RPMs. Honda’s V6 engines pair up the i-VTEC design with Variable Cylinder Management (VCM), which shuts down three or even four cylinders during light-load, steady RPM situations such as highway cruising. Honda now also offers turbo four-cyliners with i-VTEC for even more performance and power.
VTEC adds a layer of complexity to any engine, and it does sometimes come with some service bugs, despite Honda’s reputation for reliability.

- Low oil volume or dirty oil can affect operation, since VTEC relies on oil pressure to lock the rocker arms together with the more aggressive cam lobe. Low oil levels or contaminated oil can starve the system.
- Dirty oil can contaminate and clog the tiny mesh filter behind the VTEC solenoid.
- VTEC solenoids and pressure switches have been known to fail or become stuck mechanically.
- In some instances, a failed pressure switch or sensor fault can limit RPMs to about 3000, triggering limp mode and an illuminated CEL.

These problems can register trouble codes P1259/P1253 (system malfunction or circuit failure), P2646/P2647 (rockers oil pressure switch circuit low/high) or OBD1 codes 21 or 22 (VTEC solenoid valve or VTEC oil pressure switch).

If you suspect a solenoid issue, touch a 12v jumper wire to the solenoid terminal; even with the engine off, you should hear a click as the internal plunger moves. In many cases, the pickup screen for the solenoid can be cleaned of gunk and debris with Brakleen. Drivability symptoms can include rough idle, stalling, limp mode, bucking and sputtering, loss of power and, in some cases, trouble codes for emissions or traction control. It’s important to remember to let the engine get up to operating temperature before attempting any troubleshooting.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Honda’s cylinder deactivation has come with its share of problems. Even though the deactivated cylinders aren’t firing, they’re still creating a vacuum that can draw oil past the piston rings and oil control ring and up into the combustion chamber. Common issues include oil consumption, fouled spark plugs, misfires and even piston ring and catalytic converter damage. Drivers also report harshness and vibration due to an altered engine balance, wearing out hydraulic motor mounts prematurely. The oil burning and piston ring wear issues have even resulted in a class action lawsuit that Honda has had to follow up on, as well as numerous technical service bulletins. Coolant-sensor bypass devices are available to trick the engine management computer into shutting down the VCM feature and keeping all cylinders firing, compromising fuel economy in favor of engine longevity and smoothness.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The VCM system settlement covered Accord models (2008-2012), Odyssey models (2008-2013), Pilot models (2009-2013) and Crosstour models (2010-2012). As part of that settlement, Honda extended the powertrain warranty to eight years and unlimited mileage and reimbursed customers for out-of-pocket expenses related to diagnostics and repairs.

A separate lawsuit covers the 3.5L J35 V6 from model years 2016-2023 in models that include the Ridgeline, Pilot, Odyssey and Passport as well as the Acura MDX and TLX. This one stems from improperly ground crankshaft pins that can lead to premature bearing, piston and rod failure. Complaints have ranged from roughness to knocking, ticking, metal shavings in the oil filter and even complete engine seizure.

articles.title: Tighter Inventory Pushes Used Class 8 Prices Higher
articles.author: Kevin Linger

paras.en: Used Class 8 truck sales fell sharply in August even as average retail prices continued to rise, according to ACT Research. The results come from the company’s latest State of the Industry: U.S. Classes 3-8 Used Trucks report.
Same-dealer retail sales declined 24% month over month (M/M), counter to the typical seasonal increase. The average retail sale price climbed 2.2% M/M to $64,367.

Compared with August 2025, used Class 8 sales were up 12% year over year (Y/Y), while average prices increased 11% Y/Y. ACT said the August used Class 8 sales decline appears to reflect tightening inventory rather than weakening demand.
“The notable drop in used Class 8 sales this month is not necessarily a reflection of weaker demand, but more likely a result of tightening inventory,” said Steve Tam, vice president at ACT Research.
Fewer Trucks Are Reaching the Used Market
Tam said dealers across the country are reporting increasing difficulty sourcing used trucks.

ACT’s review of multiple advertising sources also showed available inventory falling meaningfully from earlier in the year. New truck sales are running below last year’s pace, which means fewer trade-ins are entering the used market, according to ACT.
“With new truck sales also running below last year’s pace, fewer trades are making their way into the used market, supporting higher prices despite lower sales volumes,” Tam said.
That supply dynamic helps explain why average used truck prices continued to rise even as August sales declined.

articles.title: Ride Sharing Market to Hit $317.47B by 2033
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The ride sharing market is projected to reach $317.47 billion by 2033, up from $170.56 billion in 2026, at a CAGR of 9.3%, according to MarketsandMarkets.

Growth is being driven by a shift from occasional ride booking toward high-frequency, platform-based mobility consumption. The user base is expanding, and trips per user are increasing. The expansion of the addressable trip pool also supports growth as platforms add lower-cost products, premium services, scheduled mobility, corporate transportation, and specialized passenger services to capture diverse trip occasions and income segments.
Platform Usage and Trip Frequency Are Increasing
Ride sharing demand is expanding through higher trip frequency and broader platform usage.

- Uber recorded 3.9 billion trips in Q2 2026, up 18% year over year, while monthly active platform consumers increased 16% to 208 million. Trips per monthly active consumer also increased 2%, indicating growth is supported by both user additions and greater usage among existing customers.

- DiDi recorded 13.74 billion China Mobility transactions in 2025, up 10.8% from 2024, while its international transactions increased from 3.61 billion to 4.51 billion, up 24.7%. This reflects continued expansion across established and international markets.

- Lyft completed 945.5 million rides in 2025, up 14%, while annual riders reached 51.3 million. Product expansion into family mobility, premium ground transportation, and other multimodal services is allowing platforms to capture travel occasions that extend beyond conventional daily ride hailing.
Multi-Use Mobility Platforms Are Expanding Addressable Demand

Ride sharing is being shaped by deeper usage within existing markets and faster expansion into new mobility demand pools. Higher trip frequency is encouraging platforms to improve vehicle utilization, while international expansion is opening additional transaction pools beyond mature markets.

Broader service offerings are allowing platforms to address different travel requirements, from daily commuting and airport travel to corporate mobility, family transportation, and short-distance urban trips. The industry is moving from a single-service model toward multi-use mobility platforms, where growth depends on increasing the number of travel occasions captured per user and expanding access across cities, customer segments, and transport modes.

He will also discuss his subsequent career as an entrepreneur, investor and business leader.

Rodriguez serves as chairman and CEO of A-Rod Corp, an investment firm. The firm backs startups and partners with global companies across real estate, sports and entertainment. Rodriguez was selected to 14 MLB All-Star teams and won the 2009 World Series with the New York Yankees. He later transitioned into business leadership and became co-chairman of the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx.

He also serves as an Emmy Award-winning MLB analyst for Fox Sports. articles.title: How did Roman aqueducts get water to go uphill?
articles.author: Owen Jarus

paras.en: Aqueducts are some of the ancient Romans' most prominent surviving archaeological remains. These aqueducts relied on gravity to bring down the water to cities gradually. But some, such as the aqueduct at Aspendos in Turkey, had sections where they had to go uphill. So how did the Romans get water to flow upward?
The Romans used a few methods, including siphons and various water-lifting devices, experts told Live Science.
One strategy was a system called an inverted siphon (sometimes simply called a siphon).

At Aspendos, in southern Turkey, there is a second-century-A.D. Roman aqueduct with inverted siphons that scholars have reconstructed with a virtual modeling simulation. To get water through a valley, the Romans built a "header tank" on one end of the valley and a slightly lower "receiving tank" (or "outlet tank") on the other side. In the valley, they constructed two towers between the tanks, Paul Kessener, a researcher in the Department of Language and Culture Studies at Radboud University in the Netherlands, noted in an article published in 2000 in the Journal of Roman Archaeology.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As water dropped down a steep hill, the resulting pressure pushed it up the first tower before dropping it steeply down the other side, with the force allowing it to climb the second tower. The water eventually reached the receiving tank on the other side of the valley and continued toward the city of Aspendos.

It was important to prevent air pockets from forming as the water went through the inverted siphons. The header and receiving tanks were relatively large, allowing air bubbles to escape, Giovanni De Feo, a professor of industrial engineering at the University of Salerno in Italy, noted in an email.

"As the flow entered a relatively large chamber, its velocity decreased, allowing air bubbles to rise naturally to the water surface and escape through the open top of the structure," De Feo explained. This reduced the risk of air pockets forming.
Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The Romans tried to avoid using inverted siphons, said Charles Ortloff, a research associate in the Department of Anthropology at the University of Chicago who has a background in both engineering and history. When "Roman engineers encounter a valley, rather than construct a siphon, they [preferred] to build a bridge with a top channel to cross a valley," Ortloff said in an email. One example of this is at the Segovia aqueduct in Spain, which has a stunning bridge that still survives today.
While the Romans used inverted siphons to move water upward in an aqueduct, they employed other devices to push water out.

Perhaps the best known of these devices is the Archimedes screw, which was sometimes used to help lift water from rivers to fields. (It was allegedly designed by Archimedes, a Greek inventor who lived during the third century B.C. However, it might have actually been invented at an earlier time, noted historians Stephanie Dalley and John Peter Oleson in a 2003 paper.) When "turned by use of animal power, [it] can effectively raise water from lower river heights to higher land area heights," Ortloff said.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Archimedes screw "consisted of a wooden shaft that had [curves] of thin and flexible willow or wicker branches one stuck on top of the other, so that an endless screw was created," the Kotsanas Museum of Ancient Greek Technology's website notes. This screw was placed within a wooden pipe, and the "device was placed in the water with an inclination of 30 degrees," the museum representatives wrote. As the screw was rotated, it lifted the water.

Water wheels were also used to lift water, including in Roman mines. "The water wheel is a device that raises water and that is made up of several buckets that are fastened to a big wheel," scientists wrote in a 2024 paper. This "kind of wheel resembles a carriage wheel but it is larger and features buckets to catch water in addition to its larger size," they explained.

Another device, sometimes known as Ctesibius' pump, "was hand-moved, operating a wooden lever with a swinging motion," the scientists wrote. It had two cylinders connected to a central chamber through pistons, and the driven water exited through a nozzle connected to the central chamber.
Whatever method was used, the Romans would not let an uphill climb stop them from bringing water where they wanted it to go.

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

articles.title: 'Swamp-like colors' on the moon: NASA report reveals strange sights from Artemis II mission
articles.author: Brandon Specktor

paras.en: What it is: A view of the moon from the Artemis II crew
Where it is: Aristarchus Plateau, on the moon's near side
What color is the moon? Ask an Earthling, and you'll get a predictably monochromatic answer: white or gray.

But ask the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission — who spent nearly seven hours circling the moon from just 4,000 miles (6,400 kilometers) from the lunar surface this April — and you'll wonder if they're talking about the same dusty satellite we can see from Earth.

Yellow, brown, green, blue and tan features fan across vast volcanic plains and lurk at the edges of ominous craters, according to the crew's in-the-moment observations, which were shared this week in NASA's Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report. The 130-page document catalogs everything crewmembers Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen saw during their historic close flyby of the moon on April 6, drawing from 814 gigabytes of photo, video and audio recordings taken from the Orion crew capsule.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This rainbow of lunar color represents distinct geological features that could inform future missions on where to land and where to explore as the world's space agencies race to set up a permanent presence on the moon.

One spot that particularly enthralled the astronauts (and is featured in the image above) is the Aristarchus Plateau — a broad, elevated region on the northwestern edge of the moon's nearside. The region hosts one of the moon's densest collections of ancient volcanic features, including swaths of dark lava deposits and colorful volcanic glasses.

Koch, mission specialist for Artemis II, was shocked to see distinct yellow shades in the region; she likened the plateau to "a yellow snow-capped mountain," with sunlight-reflecting craters providing the bright "snow." She went on to call the region "a jaundiced cheek of the Moon."

"There are so many colors now," Glover, Artemis II's pilot, added while photographing the area. "There's also a green. I see brown, especially Aristarchus and north toward the north pole. … It kind of flows down from the north in brown streaks."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to the report authors, these colorful hues "could be associated with orange (titanium-rich) and green (magnesium-rich) glass beads respectively," similar to volcanic glass beads collected by the Apollo 15 and 17 missions on separate parts of the moon.

Another colorful patch of the lunar surface that caught the crew's attention was Orientale Basin — a huge, young and multiringed impact crater that's about three times as wide as Massachusetts, according to NASA. Straddling the moon's near and far sides, this massive bull's-eye is rarely visible from Earth, but it dominated the crewmembers' field of view as they orbited around the side of the moon.
"It has just created chaos across that entire area," Wiseman, commander for the mission, said at the time.

When flying over this sprawling basin, the crew noted gray, brown, tan and green below. The largest, outermost ring in the basin contained "almost swamp-like colors," Koch reported, while Glover spotted what looked like "dusted peaks" and "white on the very edges of [the mountains], the spines, the ridgebacks." Chains of craters parading away from the impact site looked "like bubbles rising from a team of scuba divers below," Koch added.

While these may sound like off-the-cuff observations, the Artemis II crew spent more than two years training to study and describe the moon's geology. Their regimen included visiting craters on Earth, taking lessons individually and in classrooms, conducting simulated flybys and, according to the report, bringing "self-selected reference materials" into the Orion capsule to read on the way to the moon.
- Earth-based telescope shares image of Artemis II capsule near the moon — one of the farthest photos of humans ever taken
- Artemis II crew captures rare double auroras on the dark side of Earth as they zoom toward the moon — Space photo of the week
- NASA just released 12,000 more Artemis II photos — here are a dozen of our favorites
Thanks to this training, the crew's observations provided a wealth of scientific information that no autonomous camera or orbiter could, the report said.

"The Artemis II mission demonstrated the exceptional value of human observation and cognition as scientific assets in planetary exploration," the report authors concluded. "Unlike cameras, which capture isolated moments and often narrow subsets of a scene, human observers continuously interpret their surroundings, integrating realtime visual perception with contextual understanding."
Or, to put that in Glover's more relatable words to mission control, "It's quite a wicked view."

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

articles.title: 'News reports tweaked the science to speak to contemporary anxieties': How Neanderthal extinction is a projection of our own, modern fears
articles.author: Peter Sahlins

paras.en: Since the discovery of their remains in the 19th century, Neanderthals have fascinated scientists and the general public alike. Although our understanding of these ancient hominins has been transformed tremendously since then, how we have viewed this other human lineage became deeply entrenched in how we see our own species, with geopolitical events shaping the rhetoric around our ancient relatives.

In his new book, "Neanderthals Among Us: The Making of a Prehistoric Human" (Oneworld Publications, 2026), historian and author Peter Sahlins examines our complicated view of Neanderthals, with this lost human lineage being viewed through the lens of cultural and political ideologies. In this excerpt, he looks at our theories for why they went extinct and the philosophical reckoning we've placed up on them.

Between violent extermination and peaceful absorption — with cultural exchange — prehistorians and others propose a wide range of theories to account for Neanderthals' extinction. Just as we've projected our concerns and anxieties about race and gender onto Neanderthals, so too do contemporary challenges shape how we imagine their extinction.

Sometimes it's the newspapers that translate a more neutral science into easily relatable headlines. "Immigrants Halt Neanderthal Era," announced the Glasgow Herald (29 July 2011), claiming that "Europe's earliest residents may have been crowded out by uncontrolled immigration 40,000 years ago." Glossing a highly technical study by Cambridge archaeologist Paul Mellars about the notable increase in population size during the Upper Palaeolithic, the news reports tweaked the science to speak to contemporary anxieties.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But often the science itself is framed or informed by current events. The pathogen thesis gained credence during and after the COVID-19 epidemic. A 2024 study of a 50,000-year-old case of herpes in a sequenced viral genome confirmed widespread speculation that Sapiens-borne pathogens were passed to a Neanderthal population without immunities. Jonathan Kennedy's popular world history "Pathogenesis" (Crown, 2023) argued that Homo sapiens would have been less vulnerable to Neanderthal diseases because they arrived in much larger numbers and had more evolved immune systems from their tropical environment.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Of growing importance over the last twenty years is the thesis that climate change, our own existential challenge of the Anthropocene, was the principal cause of Neanderthal extinction. The idea takes many shapes, beginning with an update of French geologist Georges Cuvier's "catastrophism," where species died off in cataclysmic geological events like earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Since 2007, researchers point to the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption near Naples (Italy), now dated to around 39,280 BP [before present] (+/- 110 years), fictionalised in the 2013 animated film The Croods.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Scientists argue that arriving Homo sapiens were not as affected, perhaps because there were fewer directly touched by the 120 cubic miles [500 cubic kilometers] of magma released, or perhaps because almost everyone died out — but waves of Sapiens arrived later. After all, while most of us share small parts of the Neanderthal genome, the lineages from which we 'directly' descend settled much later in Europe — long after the Ice Age. By far, the greatest portion of our genome comes from our Neolithic, not Palaeolithic, ancestors.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But perhaps "Climate Change Killed the Neanderthals," that is, the extreme climatic fluctuations during the Upper Pleistocene that National Geographic (9 February 2004) announced, following the work of an international team of thirty scientists who laboured for more than seven years on the study. The team identified a general climatic instability during the Middle Palaeolithic marked by a severe cooling event around 41,000 years ago, lasting six centuries — interstadials GIS 13 to 7 of the Greenland ice-core records, to be precise.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For the last twenty years, scientists have sought to specify the timing, magnitude and ecological impact of a "mini-Ice Age" — the prehistorical obverse of global warming — that reduced vegetation and herbivore food sources, forcing Neanderthals towards warmer climates, including southern Spain. Clive Finlayson, trained as a zoologist, was an early contributor to sophisticated ecological modeling of Neanderthal extinction. At Gibraltar, he argued, "the last Neanderthal" could be found as late as 29,000 years ago, but there's competition for the title: elsewhere in the southern climatic refugium, Zafarraya (Granada) yielded a skeleton dated to 30,000 BP, but there are skeptics, while other candidates come from the Mezmaiskaya Caves in the Caucasus.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The trope, we've seen, is a frequent one in Neanderthal fiction, including Claire Cameron's "The Last Neanderthal" (Little Brown & Co., 2017), a moving, feminist revision of "Neanderthal Woman." It's also been widely used in popular nonfiction, including in Ludovic Slimak's 2023 account of twenty-five years of research in the Mandrin Cave .

Some of the science blaming climate change for the demise of Neanderthals marks a retreat from the recent archaeological rehabilitation of Neanderthals as a type of human equal to Homo sapiens, as these theories need to account for Sapiens' survival in the same severe conditions. Some experts rewrite basic wisdom, arguing that Neanderthals were not a cold-adapted species, since their origins lay during a warm interglacial stage (MIS 11); or that they lacked the technologies for making complex (and warm) clothing; or perhaps that their preexisting biological cold adaptations delayed the development of such technologies — a story about their technological inertia and deep conservatism.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That Neanderthals died out because of their conservatism, while humans alone mastered innovation, and with it, conquered the world, is the principal claim in Philip Lieberman's "The Unpredictable Species: What Makes Humans Unique" (Princeton University Press, 2013), and it's a widely shared belief.
- Adversity shaped our evolution as a species. People raised in it may have underrecognized strengths because of it.
- 'More Neanderthal than human': How DNA from our long-lost ancestors affects our health today
- Scientists claimed the world's oldest rock art is 67,800 years old. But is the science behind that estimate flawed?

Aside from the fact that the high value placed on "innovation" corresponds to the ideological superstructure of contemporary neoliberalism and late-stage capitalism, it seems fitting that Neanderthals died out because, in this view, they were, well, truly Neanderthal. The rhetorical figure returns to haunt the science: Neanderthals were conservative, backward, clinging mindlessly to the past in a changing world.

Neanderthal conservatism — not rhetorically, but as an original character trait — has origins in nineteenth-century anthropological judgements about "primitive" peoples. Augustus Pitt Rivers, an early innovator in British archaeology, underscored "the form of a persistent conservatism" of indigenous peoples, and quoted approvingly his colleague E. B. Tylor's "Primitive Culture" (1871): "The savage is firmly, obstinately conservative. No man appeals with more unhesitating confidence to the great precedent-makers of the past; the wisdom of his ancestors can control against the most obvious evidence of his own opinions and actions."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Just as "savages" were once seen as descendants of Neanderthals, so too is their conservatism a cultural legacy, even when anthropologists, transcending an outdated comparative method, no longer deem them ancestral, or even savage.
NEANDERTHALS AMONG US: The Making of a Prehistoric Human by Peter Sahlins is published by Oneworld, hardback £28.
Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

In "Neanderthals Among Us," historian Peter Sahlins offers a sweeping interdisciplinary history of an obsession that has made Neanderthals into a distorting mirror of our claims to human uniqueness and our anxieties about human difference.

At their discovery, Neanderthals helped invent prehistory itself, saturated with racial science; initially cast as ugly, stupid, and hairy, they underwent a long and uneven rehabilitation, with science and popular culture moving at different speeds, and sometimes in opposite directions.

The reputation of “Neanderthal Man,” our Paleolithic double, has been in constant flux, remaining a site of endless fascination and debate about human uniqueness, race, gender, and the very look of the human.

Peter Sahlins is Professor of History Emeritus at University of California, Berkeley. The son of renowned anthropologist Marshall Sahlins, Peter studied early modern French and European history at Harvard and Princeton, then taught for thirty years at the University of California, Berkeley. He has written six books and scores of articles on a range of topics, most recently "1668: The Year of the Animal in France". He divides his time between Paris and Arcy-sur-Cure in Burgundy, where he also gives guided tours of its famous prehistoric caves.

articles.title: Canadian Poet Anne Carson Brings Ancient Wisdom to Modern Audiences. Now, She's a Nobel Laureate in Literature

paras.en: Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for her genre-bending works that range from poetry and ancient Greek translations to collaborations with dancers and musicians.

The Swedish Academy recognized the 76-year-old Canadian poet, essayist and translator on October 8 for “her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

Throughout her career, Carson has repeatedly taken texts and ideas from the ancient world and made them feel contemporary, using unconventional forms and a modern voice to probe enduring questions about love, loss, desire and identity.

The Nobel Committee for Literature praised Carson’s boundary-defying approach, which has led “to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and art forms,” chair Anders Olsson said during the award announcement.

Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, also complimented Carson’s unique style, saying in a statement that by “drawing on ancient traditions with bold imagination and originality,” Carson had “reimagined the classics with wit, imagination and a style entirely her own.”
Carney adds, “She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature.”

Carson’s 1986 debut book-length essay, Eros the Bittersweet, examined the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, while “The Glass Essay,” a long, lyrical poem published in 1995, explored the aftermath of unrequited love and grief.

The author brought a similarly inventive approach to Autobiography of Red, her 1998 verse novel that transformed the myth of Heracles and the giant Geryon into a coming-of-age story about a gay teenager and his heartbreaking romance. The book has sold nearly 100,000 copies in the United States, according to its publisher. Red Doc>, published in 2013, resumes the story, following the now-middle-aged characters on a road trip.

Carson’s work has continued to move freely between poetry, prose, myth and biography. Men in the Off Hours, a 2000 collection of poetry and prose, won Canada’s inaugural Griffin Poetry Prize, while the performance piece Norma Jeane Baker of Troy brought together the stories of two women separated by thousands of years: Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.

Carson’s 2024 poetry collection, Wrong Norma, a finalist for a National Book Award, ranged from compositions about her father to pieces about snow and Roget’s Thesaurus. The subjects had no obvious connection. “That’s why I’ve called them ‘wrong,’” the poet told the Nation’s Emily Wilson in 2024.

Over the years, Carson has “moved closer to bizarreness for the sake of bizarreness,” Daisy Fried wrote in a 2013 review of Red Doc> for the New York Times. “But she still pulls it off, mainly because the impulse behind it is mischief. ‘Can I get away with this?’ she seems to ask. And she does—because it’s fun. She’s having fun.”

Carson has also translated and reimagined foundational works of ancient Greek literature, including fragments by the poet Sappho in If Not, Winter; Sophocles’ plays Electra and Antigone; and Euripides’ The Bacchae. The Nobel Committee praised these translations as “independent works in their own right.”
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson discovered ancient Greek texts in high school and quickly became fascinated with the language.

“[It] seems different than other languages,” Carson told NPR’s Scott Simon in 2016. “It seems, somehow, more original, more like being in the morning of language. And that’s partly because the words are new. Those people are inventing ways of thinking about stuff, but also because we have thousands of years of building the words into other things, using their words to build out our words.”

Carson studied at the University of Toronto, then taught classics at the University of Calgary and McGill University while establishing herself as a writer. As her career blossomed, Carson also held positions at the University of Michigan, Princeton University, Cornell University and New York University.
In 2024, Carson, who rarely shares much about her personal life, revealed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease and had taken up boxing to help manage the condition.

“When I try to produce a complicated movement like a one-two-four-five combination in boxing (left jab, right cross, right hook, left uppercut), I can feel the neurons in my brain struggling and striving,” Carson wrote in an essay for the London Review of Books. “Yes, I can feel it.”

Carson and her partner, visual artist Robert Currie, live part-time in Iceland, where they gained citizenship in 2022. “She means a lot to the scene here,” Ragnar Kjartansson, a multidisciplinary Icelandic artist, tells the New York Times’ Alex Marshall. “She’s a force, and everyone’s really happy.”
When Ingrid Carlberg, the Swedish Academy’s secretary, called Carson to deliver the good news, the poet said she was in Iceland “listening to the wind.”
“She was taken by surprise but very happy,” Carlberg said during a livestream of the award announcement.
Later, in a telephone interview with the Nobel Prize’s outreach team, Carson reiterated that winning the award “seems a little insane. I think you’re all insane.”

The Nobel committees are announcing the winners of their six award categories this month, starting with the prize in physiology or medicine on October 5 and ending with the economics prize on October 12. Each award comes with a cash prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, a Pioneering Software Engineer Who Made the First Human Moon Landing Possible, Dies at 90

paras.en: Software engineering pioneer Margaret Hamilton died on September 30 at age 90, leaving behind a trailblazing legacy of problem-solving and entrepreneurship that paved the way for a new branch of computer science and engineering.

Hamilton is best known for her major contributions to the Apollo missions. Her work famously resolved a computer issue that enabled NASA’s Apollo 11 mission to put humans on the moon for the first time.

“Her coding foresight and prowess really made that mission a success,” Andrew Meade McGee, curator of computing at Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, tells Smithsonian magazine. Her impact goes far beyond the lunar landing, though, and has had long-lasting effects, he adds. “She created the logical software basis for many of the critical systems we use to maintain our infrastructure today, and that silently power today’s modern aerospace world.”

Hamilton was not widely recognized outside of computing and aerospace circles until about 20 years ago, and in 2016, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, McGee says. “A generation of coders and young women in STEM came to see her as a pioneer.”

Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936. After earning her bachelor’s degree in mathematics from Earlham College in 1958, she and her husband moved to Massachusetts. Hamilton started working on weather prediction software at MIT with Edward N. Lorenz, the meteorologist who founded chaos theory. This position marked the beginning of her computer programming journey.
In 1965, she joined the Instrumentation Lab at MIT, which was tasked with developing the onboard flight software for the Apollo program, with the goal of sending humans to the moon.

“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” Hamilton told the Guardian’s Zoë Corbyn in 2019. “Male engineers were already working on the project, but they were hardware engineers, and it wasn’t their thing. I had [software writing] as my background. I think [the lab] just figured that I could handle the unknown.”
Hamilton eventually became the lead of the team creating the on-board flight software for the crewed missions and then assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team.

Her signature work in the field was “defensive” programming—computer programs capable of predicting or fixing issues by themselves—and “priority-driven” software. The approach played a major role in the first human moon landing in July 1969. Shortly before the landing module was supposed to reach the lunar surface, alarms sounded from the onboard computer. A fault in a hardware switch had caused the computer to overload, threatening the success of the mission.

Thankfully, Hamilton and her colleagues’ priority-driven software turned off unnecessary background tasks to make room for top-priority tasks, and the mission was able to carry on. “I was not concentrating on the mission per se, I was concentrating on the software,” she explained in an interview with Makers in 2017. “All of a sudden, it was like everything you did on Apollo to that point in time, it just all happened in front of you. People say that before they’re no longer here, they see their life. I could see the Apollo life. Just, my god, look what happened. We did it. It worked.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: No issues were ever found in any of the Apollo guidance software overseen by Hamilton, according to the Wall Street Journal’s Robert Lee Hotz. What’s more, Hamilton popularized the term software engineering.

“I fought to bring the software legitimacy so that it—and those building it—would be given its due respect, and thus I began to use the term ‘software engineering’ to distinguish it from hardware and other kinds of engineering, yet treat each type of engineering as part of the overall systems engineering process,” Hamilton told El Pais’ Javier Pedreira in 2017, per a translation cited by MIT. “When I first started using this phrase, it was considered to be quite amusing.”

In 1976, Hamilton founded the software company Higher Order Software. A decade later, she founded her second software company, Hamilton Technologies. She is an author of more than 130 publications, according to MIT.

In 2003, she was honored with a NASA Exceptional Space Act Award for her scientific and technical contributions. Hamilton also won the Computer History Museum Fellow Award in 2017 and the Intrepid Lifetime Achievement Award in 2019, and she was inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame in 2022. The Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum awarded her the 2025 Michael Collins Trophy for lifetime achievement.
Hamilton was even immortalized in Lego’s now-retired Women of NASA set. She is survived by three siblings, her daughter, son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren.

articles.title: J.M.W. Turner Painted This Breathtaking Roman Landscape Nearly 200 Years Ago. If You Look Closely, You Can Still See His Fingerprints

paras.en: When J.M.W. Turner landed a commission to paint Rome in the early 19th century, his patron gave him specific instructions: He was to capture the city authentically, showing modern life beside the ancient ruins. The piece should be “‘a copy,’ not an ideal picture,” according to an early Turner biographer, and the artist was “particularly anxious to comply.”

The patron, Hugh Andrew Johnstone Munro of Novar, kept Rome, From Mount Aventine for the rest of his life. After he died, the painting was purchased by Archibald Primrose, who would later become the British prime minister. It remained with his descendants until 2014, when it sold for $47.4 million, becoming the most expensive Turner ever auctioned.

Now, it’s up for grabs once again. On December 9, the landscape will appear at a much-anticipated Sotheby’s auction, where it’s expected to fetch a record-breaking $66 million. Accounting for inflation, this estimate is about 15 percent higher than the 2014 price.

“As an artist, Turner is at his best when working with a subject that has close personal meaning, and no subject could be closer to his heart than Rome,” Julian Gascoigne, a senior director at Sotheby’s, writes in an essay. “In all my years in the art world, few other works have appeared that are as exceptional as this.”

Nearly 200 years later, the canvas still bears evidence of the Romantic artist’s energetic handiwork: Small hairs from his brush and marks from his palette knife are visible. Viewers can even make out some of his fingerprints. The painting will be sold in its original frame, and it’s one of only two late Turners that remain unlined.

- “Lining” is a treatment that involves attaching new fabric to the back of a painting to support its original canvas. This process can also cause damage, and it’s been the subject of extensive debate among conservators.

- “Lining is a major treatment, which should only be carried out when absolutely necessary,” according to Royal Museums Greenwich. “The 1974 Greenwich Lining Conference sought to broker an international agreement on how and when to carry out the process.”

Ahead of the auction, the painting went on display in Rome for a few days last week. It will now travel to London, Hong Kong and New York. Mario Tavella, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, tells Agence France-Presse that he hopes the piece will find its way to a museum “where it could be admired by everyone.”

Born in London in 1775, Turner started painting as a boy, and his father proudly displayed his creations in the barbershop where he worked. He was accepted into the Royal Academy at age 14, and he studied paintings and sculptures by famous Italian artists years before he traveled to the country. With time, “his works became more and more expressive,” per the Ashmolean Museum, “with some bordering on abstract as form, and detail became secondary to the mood of the scene.” Today, the so-called painter of light is known for his sweeping landscapes and dramatic colors.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Turner was revolutionary. He broke down the formal structure of the painting and moved toward forms that are looser and more abstract,” Gascoigne tells Artnet’s Richard Whiddington. “It’s a new vision of what painting can be and how we should perceive the painted image.”

Experts aren’t sure exactly when Munro commissioned Rome, From Mount Aventine. According to a statement from Sotheby’s, Turner started working on the painting in the late 1820s, when he traveled to the city and completed five detailed studies. He later finished the scene in London. The landscape shows the Tiber River flowing through the bustling city, which is lit by brilliant yellow sunshine. Turner added a priest and a young girl in the foreground beneath a towering umbrella pine.

In 1836, the painting went on view at the Royal Academy, where it sparked heated disagreements. “There was a group of critics who did not ‘get’ him, who thought his coloring was crude and sloppy and didn’t understand his fascination with light and atmosphere,” Gascoigne tells the London Times’ Tom Kington. “Others, however, saw him as a revolutionary genius.”

articles.title: Hurricane Simon weakens to Cat. 1 storm along Mexico's west coast

paras.en: Oct. 13 (UPI) -- Hurricane Simon weakened to a Category 1 storm late Monday, as it moved slowly northwest along Mexico's west coast, lashing the region with heavy rain and flooding, forecasters said.

The storm was located about 90 miles west of Cabo Corrientes, Mexico, and 190 miles south of Mazatlan, Mexico, the NHC said in its 11 p.m. MST update. The storm had maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, a drop of 10 mph in three hours.
It was moving northwest at a 3 mph crawl.

A hurricane warning was in effect for Las Islas Marias, while a hurricane watch was in effect for north of Escuinapa to Bahia Tempehuaya. A tropical storm watch was also in effect for Cabo Corrientes to Escuinapa.
"Simon is expected to continue moving slowly northwestward during the next day or so, followed by a turn toward the north on Wednesday," the NHC said.
"Some additional weakening is forecast over the next day or so, but Simon is forecast to remain a hurricane through midweek and could re-intensify by Wednesday."
Simon was likely to produce rainfall totals of 5 to 10 inches across coastal west-central Mexico. Isolated maximum amounts of 15 inches were possible over Sinaloa by Thursday.
Storm surge was possible along the immediate coast near Las Islas Marias, the NHC said. Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves.

articles.title: On This Day, Oct. 13: Continental Congress establishes Navy

paras.en: Oct. 13 (UPI) -- On this date in history:
In 1775, the Continental Congress ordered construction of America's first naval fleet.
In 1792, the cornerstone to the White House in Washington was laid. It would be November 1800 before the first presidential family -- that of John Adams -- moved in.
In 1903, the Boston Americans (later known as the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates to win the first modern World Series, five games to three.
In 1917, up to 100,000 people gathered in Fatima, Portugal, for the "Miracle of the Sun" and its strange solar activity and, for many, a reported glimpse of the Virgin Mary.
In 1943, conquered by the Allies, Italy declared war on Germany, its Axis former partner.

In 1972, Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571 carrying 45 people, including a rugby team from Montevideo, crashed in the Andes mountains. It would take 72 days for rescuers to learn the fate of the survivors, and by that time, only 16 were left to tell their story. The survivor's harrowing story was brought to the big screen in the 1993 feature film, Alive.
In 1972, more than 170 people were killed in a Soviet airliner crash near Moscow's Sheremetyevo International Airport.

In 1987, Costa Rican President Oscar Arias Sanchez was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize -- the first winner from Central America. Arias was recognized for his work promoting democracy and peace in Central America.
In 1990, Syrian forces moved into Lebanon, removing Christian militia leader General Michel Aoun from power, effectively ending the Lebanese Civil War.

In 1994, two months after the Irish Republican Army announced a cease-fire, the Ulster Volunteer Force and Ulster Freedom Fighters, the two main paramilitary groups fighting to keep Northern Ireland with its Protestant majority in the United Kingdom, announced a cease-fire.

In 2000, the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the Nobel Peace Prize to South Korean President Kim Dae-jung for his efforts to reconcile his country with North Korea through a summit earlier in the year with counterpart Kim Jong Il.

In 2010, after more than two months entombed half a mile under the Chilean desert, the first of 33 trapped miners was pulled to safety in a narrow passageway drilled through more than 2,000 feet of rock, to be followed in the next 24 hours by the rest of the crew in a dramatic finale to a remarkable rescue mission.

In 2013, a stampede by masses of worshipers crossing a bridge over the Sindh River at a Hindu festival in India's Madhya Pradesh state killed more than 100 people and injured scores of others. A police official said people panicked as rumors spread that the bridge was collapsing.
In 2019, American Simone Biles became the most decorated gymnast in history with her record 25th gold medal at the World Championships in Stuttgart, Germany.
In 2021, Star Trek actor William Shatner, at 90, became the oldest person to go to space. He traveled with three others aboard a Blue Origin capsule and returned 11 minutes after reaching space.
In 2024, SpaceX used a tower with arms to "catch" the 20-story-tall booster for its Starship rocket for the first time.

paras.en: Amyl and the Sniffers will headline Golden Hour at Bondi Beach in 2027, in what’s being billed as the Melbourne punk band’s biggest Australian show yet.

The Grammy-nominated group tops the bill at the Fuzzy-run summer event on Thursday, March 4, with every act on the day fronted by a woman — Malyangapa and Barkindji rapper BARKAA and Western Sydney post-punk outfit Xiao Xiao join as special guests. For the 2027 shows, the band has committed ticket proceeds to a range of charities, with the Sydney donation acknowledging the local response to the Bondi attack.

The homecoming caps a breakout international stretch for Amyl and the Sniffers. Their 2024 third album Cartoon Darkness, produced by Nick Launay, debuted at No. 2 on the ARIA Albums Chart and became the band’s first entry on the Billboard 200, peaking at No. 196. The album also delivered the band’s first Grammy nomination, with its single “U Should Not Be Doing That” up for best rock performance at the 2026 ceremony, alongside a BRIT Award nomination and performances at Glastonbury and Coachella. At the 2025 ARIA Awards, the group swept four prizes including album of the year, best group and best rock album.
